en: CHAPTER I:
Demonstrating the Means for Abandoning Constant Error;
[The Two] That Occur Together.

For indeed, if union with things other than [the self] is dear to you, how can separation from those very same things not be unpleasant? Is it not the case that wherever there is union within a continuum, separation is necessarily present there as well? Thus, both union and separation are seen to be concomitants. Therefore, by one who seeks union, separation must also be accepted.

He performed worship and obtained a boon, saying, "May prosperity (Śrī) be mine. As soon as he entered his house, Prosperity entered the house and Kālakarṇī followed closely behind her. He asked Prosperity, "Who is this? She replied, "This is Kālakarṇī. He said, "I did not obtain a boon for her sake. She said, "Wherever I am, she must certainly be there. Thus, wherever there is union, there is suffering.
In this way, the happiness of every union is invariably followed by the suffering of separation.
Thus, for one who desires the consumption of the bait on the hook, the piercing and extraction by the hook are likewise inevitable.
To this, he replies: "Even though separation is certain in the end, it is not taken into account because of the greatness of the union at the beginning."
That which has passed away has neither beginning nor end, and so it is with that which is yet to come; by what means can you perceive them?

It is manifested through application. Even that which belongs to the future is of the same nature [as the present], because it has not yet been attained while ignorance still exists. Thus, for one fallen into the great ocean of saṃsāra with its beginningless and endless births, since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish at every moment, whatever conjunction there is of all these things is momentary. Therefore, since disjunction is comprised within the past and the future and is extremely subtle, when conjunction is perceived, one who perceives disjunction should always maintain a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

This is like a dispute over the abduction of another's wife. A certain man went to another country; while he was away, his wife was heard of by another man living near the village. Having heard this, he went to a brothel and lamented for her, based on that momentary separation at that particular time. Here it is asked: "Even though the separation was great, nevertheless, because his mind was captivated by the excellence of the season (*ṛtusampad*), he did not truly grieve for her. It is replied: [this is not so].
Moments and other units of time pass by like enemies according to their fixed law;
therefore, you should never feel passion toward those things that have become your enemies.

In this regard, since your life is momentary, you must become skilled in discerning those times when passion might arise within you, acting with heedfulness like one who recognizes an enemy disguised as a friend. It is like the case of an old slave-girl whose suffering was continuous; for just as her masters [punished] her for the fault of even a moment’s contempt, so too must you remain vigilant.
One desires coolness in the heat;

likewise, how could there be happiness through anything else? Thus, even while reflecting upon this nature of conditioned phenomena that stands all around us, one whose mind is agitated by spiritual urgency ought to practice what is appropriate and fitting.
What is being said?
"O evil-minded one, you do not leave your home out of fear of separation;
indeed, that which must necessarily be done, what wise man would perform it by force?"

"O evil-minded one, you do not leave your home out of fear that separation from kinsmen here is painful; yet whenever that [separation] occurs, it happens under the power of death. After experiencing great suffering, the villagers must give the entire tax, and not otherwise. Thus, kinsmen must necessarily be abandoned by death; the ignorant are made to abandon them, but they do not abandon them themselves."

Here he says: "Even if one must necessarily abandon the circle of kinsmen, nevertheless, having procreated a son and entrusted the burden of the household to him, one may depart once one has fulfilled all that was to be done."

"Or rather, I must go to the forest; however, there is some remaining duty to be performed, and having completed that, I shall go. Now, even if both that which is being done and that for the sake of which it is done must ultimately be abandoned, what benefit is there in having performed them? Therefore, this [remaining duty] is simply not to be done. Consequently, it is not appropriate to waste time out of regard for it. Thus ends the investigation into what ought and ought not to be done.

A ripe mango was taken up, and he was asked by another, "What will you do with this? He replied, "Having washed it, I shall discard it. In the same way, if sense objects are to be discarded, what is the use of investigating them? For example, a certain merchant began to rub a stone on his journey; when asked, "What are you doing?", he demonstrated that very thing [as a test] for those things to be known.
Although going to the forest is primary in terms of its purpose, nevertheless, fear arises for one who possesses attachment to self and what belongs to the self. Thus it is said:
For one who, by necessity, possesses the thought "I am a mortal," how can there be fear even of death upon the abandonment of attachment?

In this regard, for any wise person who, in accordance with the scriptures, cultivates the reflection "I am subject to death," there is no fear at all; how much less could there be fear from going to the forest or from separation from one's children? Therefore, one should apply oneself precisely to the cultivation of the recollection of death (*maraṇānusmṛti*).

It is like wearing a ring that neutralizes poison, and like the abandonment of poisoned food. For just as a ring that neutralizes poison is worn upon the hand, so too should the afflictions (*kleśa*) be dealt with by the wise.
Through renunciation, there is the supreme good.
The first chapter, the demonstration of the means for abandoning the misconception of permanence, in the *Catuḥśataka* on the Bodhisattva’s practice of yoga by the master Āryadeva, is completed.
CHAPTER II.
First, it has been stated in the first section the means for abandoning the misconception that there is permanence in the impermanent.

Because, when the body exists, there arise four hundred and four diseases originating internally, caused by the imbalance of the elements; and [there arise] those born externally, caused by contact with clods of earth, sticks, weapons, cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, reptiles, and so forth. Therefore, it is the cause for the arising of manifold sufferings.
Likewise, it becomes a vessel for suffering; moreover, it is understood because it is impossible to cultivate through happiness. For instance:
Even over a very long period of time, the body does not become its own master of happiness;
indeed, it is not logical for one thing to overcome its own inherent nature.

Even over a very long period of time, although one’s own body is attended to by various objects that serve as causes for the enjoyment of pleasure, it does not become pleasure itself, because its intrinsic nature is suffering. Just as, for example, although substances such as tin, lead, silver, and gold—which are hard by nature—attain a state of fluidity through contact with fire, yet that fluidity is never their inherent nature; their intrinsic nature remains hardness.

Because it has been stated thus, and because the body is by its very nature suffering, even over a very long period of time it is impossible to make that which is not one's own into something belonging to oneself; therefore, the body is indeed suffering.
Like the young cuckoo: just as a young cuckoo reared by a crow remains a cuckoo and not a crow, so too the body does not belong to pleasure. And on this point there is a verse:
"The body is of the nature of suffering; why do you, blinded by delusion, claim it as pleasure?
For black iron never attains the state of gold, even after a very long time."
Thus [it is said].

It might be argued: "Even though suffering exists, it does not become a source of harm if it is not perceived; for instance, some are seen to be exclusively happy from birth until death. Furthermore, the most excellent beings, having fixed their resolve upon a great state, do not experience [suffering] due to their absorption in that [state]. Therefore, how can the body be said to be essentially suffering? It is replied: "For the foremost, suffering is mental; for others, it is born of the body."
This world is struck down day after day by two kinds of suffering.

Indeed, suffering is twofold: physical and mental. Among these, for those who are endowed with all the requisites for happiness—foremost, of noble birth, and possessing great wealth—their mental suffering is constant and does not cease; for those of coarse desires, because the great status they seek is difficult to attain, they experience much envy and the pain of not obtaining what they desire. Furthermore, there are those of low birth, deprived of food, bedding, shelter, and clothing, who, due to their inferiority, are base beings.

They are indeed struck down by physical suffering; how, then, could there be any opportunity for happiness for anyone? Thus, this entire world is struck day after day by these two kinds of suffering. Therefore, herein no one exists who is happy by their very nature.

It is like the satisfaction of a supervisor who has been entrusted with the task of mounting a wild elephant. A certain king placed someone upon a difficult-to-tame elephant and commanded, "Drive it! And by him, that elephant was properly driven.

Thereupon, the king was well-pleased and honored that man. Seeing the honor bestowed upon him, the elephant official became distressed; out of fear of this, dejection arose within him. Then the king placed another inferior man upon that elephant and commanded, "Drive it! He was unable to do so, and the king subjected him to physical suffering. Consequently, satisfaction arose in the official.

In that case, one person experienced mental suffering and the second physical suffering. Likewise, for the great, mental suffering arises from being insulted, while for the lowly, it arises from being beaten. And regarding this, there is a verse:
"The world, afflicted by these two kinds of suffering, is tormented by the suffering inherent in its very nature."
Seeing this, what compassionate person could say of him, "He is happy"?
Thus it is said.

To this it is said: Even if two kinds of suffering exist, nevertheless, because they are overwhelmed by great pleasure, they are not perceived. It is replied: Whence is the greatness of that pleasure? Because even a phenomenon called "conceptualization," which is subject to suffering, has its activity obstructed. For instance:
Happiness is subject to conceptual construction, while conceptual construction is subject to suffering;
therefore, there is nothing anywhere that is more powerful than suffering.

When indeed this person conceives thus: "I am the giver, I am the lord; I enjoy the desired objects of the senses," then mental pleasure arises for him who so conceives. Even for those who are immersed in pleasure, that mental pleasure ceases again through the conceptualization of the interruption of enjoyment, as they fear its future loss. Thus, because pleasure is subject to the governance of conceptualization due to its arising and cessation, pleasure is under the control of conceptualization.
Suffering, however, is not like this; for there is no conceptual construction whatsoever that could obstruct its capacity to cause affliction.
Therefore, unlike pleasure, suffering is not dependent upon conceptual construction.

Indeed, both this pleasure derived from the enjoyment of desired objects and the conceptualization conducive to the arising of pleasure—both of these, once produced, destroy [the pleasure]. For even while one is enjoying a sense-object, if one is overcome by any kind of suffering, one abandons all that pleasure along with the conceptualization and perceives only suffering, not pleasure. Thus, because the conceptualization of pleasure is subject to suffering, suffering alone is more powerful, not pleasure;
just as [a woman] is pained by the hospitality shown to the son of a co-wife. Sapa... [text fragment]

Of two women, one was a mother whose son had died and the second was a mother who had a living son. There, the woman whose son had died saw her co-wife’s son being honored and grieved exceedingly. When she was asked, "Why do you grieve for that which is dead and beloved? she replied, "I do not grieve for him; rather, I grieve because this son of my co-wife is alive. Later, when the co-wife’s son fell ill, she went to another village.

After a few days, she arrived at that village, and a corpse was being carried out from it. She imagined that this was the very son of her rival wife who had died. Because she had constructed this mental image, an intense state of joy arose within her. However, she was bitten by a scorpion on a limb; thus, while the joy born of her mental construction arose, it was overwhelmed by the suffering of the poison. Therefore, there is nothing anywhere more powerful than suffering. And regarding this, it is said:
Since pleasure arises from perversion, it is therefore very difficult to find;
suffering, however, issues from reality, and for that reason it is far more powerful.
Thus it is said.

To this, he replies: "Even though happiness is difficult to find, nevertheless, because it does not cause affliction to the body, that [happiness] belongs to oneself; whereas even great suffering, because it causes affliction, belongs to another. It is said in response:
"In whatever manner time passes, in that same manner there is an increase of suffering."
Therefore, happiness in this physical body is seen to be like that of another.

Indeed, as the lifespan of the body increases—whether in childhood, youth, adulthood, or old age—it is observed that suffering increases accordingly, and not happiness. For as the body thus develops, happiness recedes further and further behind it; therefore, it is seen that for this body, suffering alone is its own, while happiness is something belonging to another.

It is like a long-distance traveler. Just as for a long-distance traveler there arises day by day an increasingly intense suffering of fatigue and the suffering of the exhaustion of provisions on the road, so too do all foolish ordinary persons, the longer they live, the more they encounter the suffering of old age and become ever closer to death. And regarding this, it is said:
"Because of attachment, suffering as if it were a companion constantly moves ever closer before him."
And he abandons bodily pleasure like something belonging to another; therefore, he becomes supreme.

Here he says: "Even if suffering is the inherent nature of this body, nevertheless, since there exists a remedy for the causes of pleasure, one should not feel revulsion toward one's own body. It is said in reply:
"As many diseases and other things as are seen to be causes of suffering, that many causes of pleasure are not seen among human beings."

In this world, however many causes of suffering for the body are observed—namely, diseases arising internally from the imbalance of the elements (*dhātu*), and other external ones such as undesirable contacts caused by cold and so forth—just as many causes of happiness for this body are not observed at all, whether internal or external.

Since the causes of happiness for the body are few while the causes of suffering are many, one should not fail to be repelled by suffering on the grounds that some causes of happiness exist. That is not so.

It is like the case of those who seek the hand of a king’s daughter in a *svayaṃvara*, and like Māndhātṛ’s abduction of Vaiśravaṇa’s daughter. Those who seek a king’s daughter in a *svayaṃvara* are joined with suffering; for she becomes a cause of happiness for only one person, not for all. Many seek her, yet they do not obtain her, and thus they become miserable. Likewise, for sentient beings, causes of suffering are many while causes of happiness are few.
Similarly, in the abduction of Vaiśravaṇa’s daughter, both [parties] come to have many causes of suffering, just as in the case of Māndhātṛ.
Because it is more powerful; however, the causes of pleasure are not so. And it is said in this regard:
"Pleasure is like a drop of water, while suffering is like the waters of the ocean;
having understood this regarding the body, how could a wise person consider it to be pleasure?"
Here it is said: If that which is called pleasure did not exist, its increase would not be observed; and since the increase of pleasure is observed, therefore pleasure exists. It is replied:
Just as the reversal [of the nature] of increasing pleasure is observed, there is no such reversal for increasing suffering.

For as the increase of pleasure occurs, so too is its opposite observed in that which is increasing. If pleasure were by its very nature [inherently existent], there would be no such reversal of it; however, while there is such a reversal for increasing pleasure, there is none for suffering.

For instance, pleasure, as it increases over a long period of time, becomes deprecated and arises with diminished intensity. Suffering, however, as it increases, becomes more intensely agonizing and harsh, and it strikes down both body and mind even more severely. Thus, because there is no such reversal in its increase, the body is by nature suffering; it does not exist by nature as pleasure, just like the fall of King Māndhātṛ.
Chapter III.

A certain king had his fortune-teller announce: "Rain will fall; whoever uses that water for their needs shall go mad. Then the king covered his own well for his own sake, and so that rain fell. Thereupon, the people of that region, having used that water for their needs, though they were indeed maddened, because they shared the same nature [of madness], considered themselves alone to be healthy and the king to be mad.
Then, having understood the matter, the king consumed that very water, thinking: "Lest they should suspect me of being insane and mock me, or even destroy me."

Thus, if there were only one person who passed urine, he would be shunned like a leper; but when everyone passes urine, then where will the perception of impurity arise? Furthermore, in a certain region where every person is afflicted with goiters and is extremely deformed, a handsome man arrives there and is shunned by them as being "extremely deformed" and "limb-deficient. And it is said in this regard: if the world were free from defects, everyone would be attached to it.
Since a fault does exist, therefore the virtuous abandon it.

Here it is said: "He who, having become a youth, does not with satisfaction enjoy a group of young women endowed with all necessary requisites, is utterly deceived in the world of the living. For indeed, by dwelling in the fragrance of their sweet perfumes, his own impurity is removed; thus, for those who resort to what is pure, there is no fault. To this, it is replied:
Just as someone with a missing limb might find satisfaction in a prosthetic nose,
so too is passion directed toward flowers and such things merely as a remedy for impurity.

Just as someone whose nose has been removed, wearing a prosthetic nose, considers his entire body to be whole and experiences satisfaction; for, being of a foolish nature, he produces satisfaction by means of that very prosthetic nose which he ought to feel ashamed of because it is not his own natural nose. In the same way...

Furthermore, due to delusion, there arises in the foolish person—by nature prone to craving for sensual pleasures—an intense attachment toward things that are merely remedies for impurity, such as fragrant flowers, perfumes, and ornaments, which lack the very nature of a body. Through this [attachment], he considers himself and others to be pure. For even when flowers and the like are worn, they are not able to permeate him with a lasting excellence of fragrance, just as garlic cannot perfume a person.

It is like licking the nose of a cat smeared with ghee, and like the satisfaction felt upon seeing a golden nose-ornament. For instance, when a cat’s nose has been anointed with ghee and it is given a lump of dry food, it perceives that food as being moistened by oil. And just as one whose own nose is lost might have a golden nose made and feel joy upon seeing it, so too do people produce passion for the body by using flowers and other such things to mask its impurity. As it is said in this regard: Regarding the body, which is like a wound, [people apply] perfumes, garlands, fine garments, and the like.
Out of delusion, people become passionately attached to things that serve merely as ointments for a wound.
Here it is said: "There is a cause for passion, namely flowers and the like; and if there were no cause, people would not be attached to bodies because of them. It is replied:
That which is called "pure" is not logical, since it is that from which detachment arises.
And there is no existent thing anywhere that, by necessity, is the cause of passion.

Indeed, there is no such thing as an object that is pure by its own nature (*svabhāva*). In this regard, those whose vision is unimpaired become disenchanted upon observing the body—which is a mass of excrement—as being like a vessel filled with the seeds of filth. Therefore, because it is the cause of such disenchantment, the body is not established as pure, just like a heap of feces. Likewise, flowers and the like are not necessarily established as causes of passion, for disenchantment also arises toward them; for instance, in those who have attained detachment from sensual desire (*kāma-vairāgya*), disenchantment arises even toward them.

Furthermore, by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is indeed nothing that is called "pure" which would necessarily be a cause for passion. For instance, even in the case of flowers and the like, which are perceived as pure, when they have withered, a sense of repulsiveness arises due to their transformation. If these things possessed purity by way of intrinsic nature, there would be no such transformation. Therefore, they do not possess purity by way of intrinsic nature. And if flowers and so forth were [pure] by necessity...
Or, if they were the cause of passion, then all of them would produce passion at all times; yet this is not the case. Therefore, it is not logical for flowers and the like to be the cause of passion.

It is like the sight of one’s own daughter by someone who desires her or does not desire her. A certain merchant went abroad while his daughter was still of noble birth; after some time he returned. His daughter had reached the prime of youth and was playing with other girls in a garden outside that city. Upon seeing her, a violent passion arose within him; however, when he heard, "This is your daughter," he became dispassionate.
Thus, there is no object whatsoever that invariably produces passion. And that in which dispassion arises should be understood as impure. As it is said in this regard:
Since one is attached to that very same thing and becomes detached from that very same thing,
it is established by necessity that there is no cause for passion.

Thus, since this impure body has been previously established as suffering and impermanent, its lack of self (anātmatva) will be demonstrated hereafter. These are the four non-perversions (aviparyāsa). Now it is considered: do these four non-perversions occur with respect to a single entity, or not? It is said:
impermanence, impurity, suffering, and non-self—this is the tetrad.
In short, all [elements] are possible within a single one.

Whatever is conditioned and dependently originated is impermanent because it is momentary; and whatever is impermanent is impure because it causes agitation; and whatever is impure is suffering because it causes affliction; and whatever is suffering is non-self because it lacks independence. Thus, in a single entity, these four non-perversions (aviparyāsa) occur in brief. Yet, although this is present, it is not discerned by the foolish who are perverted;
rather, they conceptualize the opposite nature of entities. Therefore, it is worthy [of investigation].

Thus, the wise person, having studied the impermanence and other characteristics of phenomena as they truly exist, in order to incite the mind toward the realization of their lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), acts like one who is terrified by the sight of a *piśācī*’s true nature. Suppose there is a certain woman established in the form of a *piśācī*’s wife; he treats her as his wife. But when he perceives her true nature—through the production of suffering, her loathsomeness, her lack of submissiveness, and her non-eternality—he becomes afraid and thinks, "This is not my wife; she is a *piśācī*. Then he becomes detached from her. In the same way, through the vision of the nature of conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*), people become detached.
The wise [say this]. And it is said here:
"That which is conditioned is not eternal; that which is impermanent is not auspicious;
that which is inauspicious is not happiness; and that which is suffering is without self."
Since the four perversions occur in relation to one and the same conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*), therefore all afflictions (*kleśa*) are without objective basis (*avastuka*).
Thus it is said.
The third chapter, titled "Reflection on Impurity."
CHAPTER IV: THE MEANS FOR ABANDONING THE ERRONEOUS NOTION OF THE I-CONSCIOUSNESS (Ahaṃkāra-viparyāsa-prahāṇopāya) I
Here it is asked: The means for abandoning the three types of inversion have been explained; now let the means for abandoning the fourth inversion be stated. It is said in reply:
For whom who exists in existence could there be the pride of "I" or "mine"?
Because all objects are common to all embodied beings.

Indeed, both the notions of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*) and "mine" (*mamakāra*) prevail excessively in a king; therefore, by means of their prohibition, the king himself is primarily instructed. Among these, *ahaṅkāra* arises from the conceptualization of a specific excellence in oneself, thinking, "I am the lord. *Mamakāra*, however, arises from the conceptualization of mastery over objects one has appropriated, thinking, "These objects are mine. *Darpa* is arrogance.

*Garva* means intoxication (*mada*). *Bhava* is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), the wandering through the five destinies by way of a succession of births and deaths for one who is dependent upon karma and afflictions. For what wise person existing therein could pride arise from the notions of "I" and "mine"? If indeed someone possessed a unique sovereignty over anything, then pride based on that would be appropriate, seeing a sense of mastery such as: "I alone am the master of these objects; these objects belong to me alone. But this is not possible for an ignorant person included within cyclic existence.

It is so; for all objects, such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, are produced by the collective karma of all sentient beings. Therefore, regarding these objects of common enjoyment—just like shared groves, pavilions, and the like—it is not appropriate to harbor pride through the grasping of "I" and "mine. It is like a royal actor: just as a royal actor in one moment becomes an actor, in another a king, in another a minister, in another a brahmin, a householder, or a slave, so too the king is unstable, because he performs the dance upon the stage of the five realms of existence (*pañcagati*). And there is a verse on this point: [Verse]... [omitted] ... It is so; for all objects, such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, are produced by the collective karma of all sentient beings. Since sovereignty or the perfection of enjoyments is obtained through merit,
pride is not fitting for a virtuous person in this world, which is composed of karma.
To this he says: Since every undertaking is entrusted to the king, it is therefore appropriate that he possess pride caused by that authority. It is replied:
What pride can there be for you, who are like a slave of the multitude, hired for a sixth part [of the produce], whether the task entrusted to you be one or another?

Even though theft had not yet arisen in the world of the first kalpa, a capable man was hired by the great multitude for the purpose of guarding the fields with a wage consisting of one-sixth of the grain; how could this not be [the origin of kingship]?

At that time, all the sites were burned by fire; many thousands of living beings were killed there, and that king rejoiced in it. Thus, wherever there is folly, compassion is not found; where there is no compassion, how can there be the attainment of merit? For kings, everything is possible; therefore, even for those who protect [the earth], dharma does not exist. And it is said:
"Since those whose nature is compassion say that non-violence is the root of dharma, therefore dharma does not exist in a merciless lord of men."
To this, it is said: "Even for a king who commits violence according to the warrior-dharma (kṣatradharma) ordained by the sages, there is no unrighteousness. To this we reply:
"A wise person should not perform every action merely because it was practiced by the sages."
Because among them as well, there exists the state of being inferior, middling, or superior.

In this world, a wise person should not perform any of the activities of body, speech, or mind that belong to the sages (*ṛṣis*), because even among the sages there exists the distinction of inferior, middling, and superior. Among them, one for whom violence is considered *dharma* due to some specific cause is inferior; one who has doubt as to whether it is *dharma* or not is middling; but one for whom violence is indeed *adharma* is superior. Therefore, the scripture of all sages is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). In that regard, whatever is desired by [the teaching] composed by the sages...
The claim that there is no unrighteousness for a king even when he inflicts injury according to the law is incorrect.

This is because of the cases of Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and Jamadagni; for theft, the eating of forbidden food, sexual intercourse with forbidden women, and the taking of life are heard of in connection with Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and Jamadagni. Among them, the theft and the eating of forbidden food are heard of in the case of Viśvāmitra. Indeed, it is said that he spoke thus while wishing to take away dog-meat from the dog-cookers (śvapacas).
"It is possible for one who is alive to cross over evil karma;
for this expiation is specifically for us.
But once dead, I shall not be able to cross over this evil."
Therefore, it is heard that Vasiṣṭha, having committed an improper act with Akṣamālā, a Caṇḍālī woman, was about to eat dog-meat; from that, it is said, sons were born.
Likewise, by Jamadagnya, out of anger at the abduction of his calf, the thousand arms of Kārtavīrya Arjuna were struck down. For thus he says:
Even for one who is self-controlled and patient, the mind of a sage— though it possesses transcendent fortitude— is forcibly provoked to indignation by various injuries inflicted by wicked people;
just as at the time of milking, a cow’s heart is made to low with distress when her calf is led away.
Those kings who entered the edge of Rāma’s perfectly stainless axe.
Thus, urged by his mother, he thrice seven times cleared the earth of the kṣatriya caste; and it is said that this was what his mother had told him.
In battle, he was upright, mild, ascetic, and most worthy of honor by hundreds;
yet he did not seek even a single thing from others that could have caused the destruction of the world.
A powerful man does not find satisfaction through an act consisting of mere harm;
O Hero, inflict a more severe torment and utterly uproot the very root of your enemies.
Thus it was said; thereafter, the sound of his bowstring being twanged was heard.
Surpassing the turrets of the ramparts and as if shattering the palaces of the kings,
that roar of Jamadagni’s bow seized Kārtavīrya by the hair, as it were.
And it is said in this regard:
"Those wise ones who seek their own welfare should not accept as authoritative that scripture by following whose teachings men, having acted upon them, would certainly go to an evil rebirth."

It is said: "Since the kings of old, having taken the meaning of the treatises as their authority, have properly protected the flourishing earth, for that reason also the treatise is an authority. To this it is replied:
The world was once protected like a son by auspicious kings; today, however,
it has been turned into a wilderness by those who have taken refuge in the ways of the Kali age.

In former times, the world was protected by kings such as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) who appeared before the Kali Yuga—men endowed with auspicious qualities, capable of discerning what is appropriate and inappropriate, who took as their authority the scriptures conducive to Dharma while rejecting those contrary to it, who were established in the ten wholesome actions, and who followed a love for the world like that for an only beloved son. But now, the world is [ruled] by kings born in the Kali Yuga who are dependent on the wickedness of their own minds, devoted solely to the thirst for wealth, who take as their authority the scriptures conducive to *adharma* while abandoning those conducive to Dharma.

This world has been rendered desolate by those devoid of compassion, as if it were turned into a wilderness for deer; for this reason also, a treatise joined with unrighteousness is not an authoritative source (*pramāṇa*). It is like the crushing of unripe sugarcane by barbarians. For when a bandit, out of delusion, crushes unripe sugarcane, he produces only what is harmful and not what is beneficial. Likewise, if a king does not protect those who ought to be protected, he gains neither worldly benefit nor benefit in the life hereafter, because he performs non-meritorious acts. And it is said: "In his own kingdom and in the kingdoms of others, there is no distinction made here [between them]."
The people become happy; therefore, that scripture has been refined by the wise.
To this it is said: "In this world, there is no unrighteousness for a king who strikes his enemies at their weak points, because this is seen as the view of the treatises. To this we reply:
If no evil exists for a king who strikes at vulnerabilities,
then it certainly does not exist for other thieves either.

If indeed there is no sin for a king who strikes at enemies or others during their vulnerabilities, then surely other thieves—besides royal robbers—who, having found some vulnerability, seize the wealth of others while acting as its guardians, should not be considered primarily sinful because they strike at vulnerabilities; for by virtue of striking at vulnerabilities, they would be the primary offenders. Yet this is not accepted [by you]. Therefore, the claim that there is no sin for a king who strikes at vulnerabilities is incorrect.

It is like the case of Prince Ajitasena. It is said that a certain minister was told by a king, "When my death occurs, you shall consecrate my brother, Prince Ajitasena. Subsequently, when that king had died, the minister—who was one who strikes at vulnerabilities—had the prince killed and seized the kingdom for himself. Consequently, his infamy was firmly established in the world as that of a man of evil conduct, and in the next world there was demerit. In the same way, [one should avoid] striking at the vulnerabilities of kings.
"How can there be neither infamy nor sin for those who owe debts? To this it is said:
"Whatever black deed has been committed, its white fruit does not arise;
for from the seed of a rotten tree, a sprout of the *campaka* flower does not grow."

Here it is said: A king experiences great satisfaction after defeating his enemies at the front of battle, beholding the abundance of wealth acquired through his own heroism and prowess. Furthermore, if his death occurs in battle, then, by the certain renunciation of his own self, he attains the state of going to heaven. To this, it is replied:
The renunciation of all one's possessions is not honored in sacrifices and the like;
I think, however, that even the renunciation of one's own self is honored in battle.

In this world, those who abandon even their entire fortune for the sake of gambling, wine, and courtesans do not become partakers of merit; because such abandonment follows from addiction, it does not please the minds of the virtuous. Likewise, the abandonment of one’s own life in battle is not honored, because it is a source of demerit. For how indeed could one, rushing forward with fury in combat, being devoid of compassion and possessing a cruel disposition toward another, raise a weapon against the head of an opponent for the purpose of striking him down?

It is appropriate to assume that one who has entered the field of vision of an enemy with weapons raised and is struck down by him goes to heaven; however, the claim that it is certain for one who dies at the front of battle to go to heaven is not so, just like the case of the Ābhīrī’s gift of her father-in-law’s body. A certain Ābhīrī woman, while her husband was away, treated her father-in-law with extreme contempt. Then, when her son returned, that old Ābhīra informed him of this matter. [The sentence or paragraph continues on the following page.]

And he spoke thus: "If your wife should again show contempt toward us, I will not dwell in your house. Although he was not afraid of women and was devoted to his father, he rebuked her and said: "If you treat your father with contempt, there is no place for you in my house; perform even what is difficult for him, and give him even what is hard to give. She made that very promise.

Then, while her husband was away on a journey, she served her father-in-law with extreme care and trepidation. Having attended to him throughout the day with excellent baths, ointments, garlands, food, drink, and other comforts, she washed his feet with warm water at night, anointed them with oil, and having removed his garments, she began to climb onto the bed naked, employing a sequence of wicked stratagems.

The elder Ābhīra said, "O sinful woman, what is this you have undertaken? The Ābhīrī replied, "I was told by my husband: 'Even if it is difficult for you to do, you must do this; even if it is difficult to give, you must give. And there is nothing more difficult than this, nor anything more difficult to give than this. The elder Ābhīra said, "This is indeed a means for escaping from here; be satisfied. I shall not stay in this house any longer," and having said this, he departed. Then his son arrived; not seeing his father, he asked his wife. She said, "Master, I have no [fault]."

He reported everything, saying, "For some time he had declined, but then he was attended to with great care by me through seasonal comforts such as bathing, ointments, food, and so forth. Thereupon, that master rebuked him and expelled him from the house; however, the father was propitiated and brought back into his own home.

Just as the gift of her own body by this Ābhīrī woman of wicked disposition was not praised, so too the abandonment of life in battle by kings of evil intent is not praised; and because it is considered wicked in the world, the giving away of all one's possessions for the sake of liquor and such things is not praised. And it is said:
"For one who dies in battle, there is a journey to the peak of Mount Meru..."
By what action does even a Brahmin become a Śūdra? I wonder by what action one is not born [into such a state].

For if even one who is not a kṣatriya were to become a kṣatriya by performing the work of a kṣatriya at present, then surely even a śūdra would become a brāhmaṇa by performing the work of a brāhmaṇa—whether receiving gifts or studying. In that case, anyone else who performs the work belonging to another would likewise be that very person. Therefore, the claim that one becomes a kṣatriya through action is not tenable.

It is like crossing to the other shore. Just as a boat goes to and comes from the other shore, those standing on both banks of the river say, "The boat has reached the other shore! The boat has reached the other shore! Yet, no such thing as a "shore" is established there. In that same way, the Brahmin or Kṣatriya is not established [as such]. If a Śūdra becomes a Kṣatriya by means of his actions, then likewise a Brāhmaṇa will become a Śūdra by means of his actions. And it is said: "One falls immediately through meat, lac, and salt."
A Brahmin who sells milk becomes a Śūdra within three days.
And so forth. It is said in this regard:
"If social classes were determined by action, then birth would not be the cause therein;
nor do these arise from both, since birth has already been refuted."

Here it is said: "Since a king, by means of his great royal sovereignty, is able over time to share that sovereignty with the great masses of people, therefore a king should desire great sovereignty. To this it is replied:
O King, there is no sharing of evil as there is of sovereignty;
what wise man would bring about his own ruin for the sake of another?

It is true that it is possible for a king to share with the great multitude the vast sovereignty he has acquired over a long period of time; however, that cannot be accomplished without causing suffering to the great multitude. And inevitably, through the suffering of the great multitude, there must be great sin, just as...

Wealth is shared, but it is not possible to share the fault accumulated for its sake; that suffering must be experienced alone. Therefore, what wise person, thinking "I shall share this with another for their small benefit," would accumulate a unique fault capable of bestowing no small misfortune and bring about his own destruction in the future? This is a ground for shame, not for pride, like the case of the buffalo, or like the butcher’s son. Just as a buffalo [acts] toward itself...

For the sake of another, one person is killed and many enjoy [the result]; yet the sin belongs to the killer alone. Likewise, for the sake of the kingdom, a king performs sinful deeds, while many enjoy [the fruits].

Likewise, a dog-cub does not kill [its mother] out of fear of unrighteousness (*adharma*). When its own kin say to it, "Kill her! Whatever unrighteousness there may be in that will be shared equally among us all," he says by way of a stratagem, "I have a great pain in my head; divide it among yourselves. They reply, "That is not possible. He says, "In that case, how can the suffering of the miserable realms (*apāya*) be shared equally? And regarding this, it is said: "That which is blameless in this world and brings happiness in the next..."
That must be performed by a person who desires happiness in the next world.
To this it is said: "In this world, since a king possesses great sovereignty, he must necessarily possess great pride. To this we reply:
Having seen others who are equal, superior, or even endowed with power,
pride born of sovereignty does not take root in the hearts of the virtuous.

One who perceives their own superiority over others would possess pride; and since that pride is unstable and depends entirely upon others, the wise do not approve of it. Therefore, having abandoned pride and desiring to bring benefit to the world, one should not despise others, whether they be teachers or masters. Acting in this way, they will surely become vessels of prosperity, because they are engaged in the service of the world.

Regarding the story of Vāsula’s wife: the wife of the Brahmin Vāsula said, "There is no woman on earth who exists in female form equal to me, yet you do not honor me with clothing and ornaments befitting me. By that means, she was introduced into the harem of King Rudra. There, seeing the maidservants, her pride in her own beauty vanished; how much more so when she saw the king's wives? Thus, seeing those who were his equals and those who were superior to him, he ought to abandon intoxication and egoism. And regarding this, it is said:
When a king is weak, it is not fitting for another king to display pride;
but when the king is equal or superior, what occasion is there for pride?
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Means for Abandoning the Perversion of Egoism.

Here it is asked: From where, then, are these excellent jewels of well-spoken words obtained—those which demonstrate the reality of worldly objects as they truly exist and serve as causes for dispassion? It is said: From the Buddhas.

To the Blessed Ones. Of what nature indeed are those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones? Through the penetration of great compassion, they are devoted to accomplishing the welfare of the entire world in every way, being in every respect irreproachable and inconceivable. For it is thus:
It is said that there is no movement whatsoever of the Buddhas that is without cause; even their very breath proceeds solely for the benefit of living beings.

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, because their actions are manifested through the force of an intention to favor the entire world, grant grace to the whole world through efforts skilled in bringing about the arising of benefit for beings—efforts that yield fruit according to conditions. Indeed, there is no movement characterized by physical motion that is not conducive to the welfare of sentient beings.

Let alone purposeful activity preceded by knowledge; even this spontaneous breathing—which proceeds from birth until death day and night, independent of the projection of any specific impelling consciousness—occurs solely for the benefit of these living beings.

For thus, the breaths of these Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having issued forth, transform above the receptacles of hell into great clouds of time, like heaps of collyrium and ointment, enchanting to the minds of the denizens of hell; they completely cover the entire circle of the hellish receptacles with a sharp, sweet, and continuous sound.

Gladdening the denizens of hell with floods of clear, sweet, and cool released water, and thereby extinguishing the fires of hell, they become a source of mental serenity for those denizens whose hearts are seized by the inquiry, "By whose power has this come upon us?"— causing their mental continuums to be won over by the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable form-body; and for those whose heaps of all unwholesome karma have been exhausted through the resulting faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One, and who, as a consequence thereof,
have projected the factors conducive to liberation, these [Bodhisattvas] are of ultimate benefit.
Even his breath proceeds solely for the benefit of living beings;

the same should be applied to other instances as well. Thus, the wise person, having discerned the defects of saṃsāra and being intent upon its destruction, should—in every way—first with devotion, fix their mind upon the Blessed Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Worlds and the repository of the jewels of well-spoken verses as they have been described.

Like a mendicant of the Pārāśara clan: a certain mendicant belonging to the Pārāśara clan went to the house of a master of mechanics. Having entered that man's home, he was invited by him, who said, "You should spend the rainy season in my house; I shall provide you with alms-food."

"I shall give it to you. He did exactly so. Beneath that palace, there were many mechanical devices for performing various mechanical tasks. Then he placed the monk inside the palace, saying, "Stay here as you wish. When the monk had gone out, the patron gave him the price of the robe and paid him his wages as a laborer. The monk said, "I have performed no work for you; why should I accept wages? The patron replied:

"You have not remained here in this house without activity for even a moment, nor have you stood still in any posture of conduct (*īryāpatha*). And he shows him the machines and the profit derived from them; that is to say, there is no posture of conduct belonging to that monk which would not be for his benefit through the operation of those machines. In the same way, there is no movement of body, speech, or mind belonging to the Blessed Buddha that would be either trivial or useless. And it is said:
"The activity of body, speech, and mind..."
For the Sage whose pure intellect is permeated with great compassion, there is neither self-interest nor lack of interest; rather,
his activity proceeds solely for the sake of the welfare of others.
Thus it is said.
And those who attend upon him transcend all calamities,
up to the fear of death. For instance,
just as the word "death" is terrifying to the entire world, so too is this [teacher].
Because it causes the separation from one's beloved life,
this word "all" (sarva) is likewise terrifying even to death.

For those who correctly practice the path of the Tathāgata transcend the boundaries of that [realm], and likewise, the seeds of such practice—the roots of virtue—are established through hearing the name of the Tathāgata.
And as it was said by the Blessed One:
"All those who shall hear my name will attain final nirvana by means of one or another of the three vehicles."

Thus it is: like a fever affecting a jailer who holds authority over imprisonment. Suppose there were a certain man appointed by the royal court as the official in charge of all prisons; and when a son was born to the king, a proclamation was made for the release of all prisoners, and at that sound, the entire world rejoiced. Yet that one jailer alone was afraid and afflicted with a fever upon hearing that announcement of the release from prison. In the same way, when the Tathāgata has appeared, the whole world is delighted, with the sole exception of Māra.
And it is said:
At the very least, he made the sound "Buddha" and sang songs.

Just as this king has gone mad due to the instability caused by the reversal of his affection, so too do the wise observe that ordinary people go mad from reflecting upon that same instability of mind resulting from the reversal of affection. For it is seen that in whatever object they have excessive attachment, in that very same object they later exhibit excessive abandonment. Therefore, who would not say that one who remains in such a state of existence is insane? And it is said in this regard:
"It is action alone that brings misfortune to a man, not madness;
for madness does not make a person act strangely in the way that action does."

Thus, because it is equal to a slaughterhouse and because it is a ground for madness, existence (*bhava*) should be avoided by the wise; and it should be abandoned by the cessation of the engagement in all karma. There exists a means for abandoning this existence, namely the exhaustion of all karma. To explain how that [exhaustion] comes about, he speaks of its means:
Seeing that pain is diminishing when there is the cessation of movement and other such activities,
the wise person therefore forms the conviction that all karma is being exhausted.

Just as pains produced by walking and so forth gradually subside through the avoidance of such activities like wandering once the force of the prior impulse has been exhausted, so too do all pains [subside] entirely through the total severance of all karma.
Then he...

A wise person, desiring the severance of all karma, exerts himself for the destruction of all karma. Likewise, another who exerts himself shall also attain that state; therefore, an intelligent person should apply effort toward *nirvāṇa*, which is to be attained through the destruction of all karma and consists in the cessation of all that is felt—just like a long-distance traveler. Just as a long-distance traveler becomes increasingly distressed the further he goes, due to the suffering of fatigue and the suffering of the exhaustion of provisions on the road, so too do the foolish, while wandering on the path of *saṃsāra*, suffer from the pain of their physical basis and from [the lack of] the beautiful...

And they are afflicted by the suffering of the exhaustion of their physical postures (*īryāpatha*). Alternatively, one who is oppressed by the suffering of traveling a long distance begins to stand; then his suffering of walking ceases. He [then] begins to sit, whereby the suffering of standing ceases, and the suffering of sitting ceases through standing. If, however, being exhausted by the suffering of sitting, he does not abandon that and begin another different posture, then the cessation of the suffering pertaining to the postures would be possible for him absolutely.
This should be stated in the same way regarding the exhaustion of all karma. Thus, in this manner, all karma—
"Exhaustion is the cause for the cessation of all suffering"; thus, the wise person should apply their intellect toward the exhaustion of all karma. Regarding this, it is said:
"Just as mental happiness is superior even to physical happiness, so too here is the happiness of the exhaustion of karma superior to the happiness of the exhaustion of the afflictions."
For this reason as well, the abandonment of cyclic existence is appropriate for the wise, because it is a cause of fear. To explain further:
When even for a single effect no beginning cause is seen,
then who would not feel fear upon seeing even a single thing’s vast expansion?

In this world, when even for a single effect—whether it be material, or arising from wind, or arising from bile—the ultimate primary cause is not seen upon prior investigation through its successive stages; and when one has thus observed in detail the infinity of even a single effect due to the beginninglessness of the world's evolution, then what person who has attained wisdom would not feel fear upon seeing the evolution of the world?
It is indeed proper that he should always be filled with revulsion toward this forest of saṃsāra, which is so immeasureably continuous, dense, and difficult to traverse.
And one should cultivate the primary exertion in accordance with the [nature of the] object, just like a jar.

For just as in the case of a jar, many conditions—such as the lump of clay, the staff, the wheel, the string, water, and human effort—are seen to be involved in its production, let alone in the production of other even more substantial objects. And it is said in this regard:
"Because time is infinite, there is no beginning to the world."
Therefore, it is impossible for a living being to fully comprehend the prior limit of suffering.
Furthermore, if this person who, desiring something, moves about due to craving were to achieve its fulfillment through that very exertion, it would be appropriate for him to move; yet,
the fulfillment of every such effect does not invariably arise from it.
Since that which is done with restraint has an end, why do you distress yourself for its sake?

For in this world, every undertaking that has been begun succeeds or fails according to necessity; yet, once accomplished, every undertaking necessarily meets with destruction. In such a case, since even after a very long time that which has been done must inevitably and necessarily perish, why should this fool be distressed for its sake?
Therefore, having cast it aside, one should strive to sever that web.

It is like the baking of a pot. Just as the success of the potter’s baking is uncertain, and once the vessels have been completed by the potter they are inevitably destroyed, so too the success of all worldly undertakings is uncertain. And it is said in this regard:
"Because all things are produced, there is no certainty of their lasting;
therefore, their destruction is necessarily and invariably certain."
And demonstrating that just as the destruction of an effect is certain, so too is that of an action, he says:
Action is performed with effort, yet once done, it perishes without effort;
even though such is the nature of action, you possess no detachment whatsoever.

Indeed, in this world, action is performed with great effort and by means of many instruments; yet that which has been accomplished through such great exertion and numerous means perishes quite effortlessly, like a mere effect. Thus, since the immense exertion of human effort is rendered useless, how could a wise person not feel detachment toward worldly action? On the contrary, your lack of detachment due to the repeated performance of such actions only betrays your dull-wittedness. Therefore, let the path to detachment be pursued; for a harsh way of life neither benefits nor shines.

It is like the placing of a stone upon a mountain. Just as a stone on a mountain peak is placed with great effort yet falls down without effort, so too are all worldly activities. And it is said in this regard:
"Since karma is conditioned by the assembly of causes and conditions, therefore whatever is performed with effort perishes through that very deficiency."
Thus [it is said].
Here he says: "Even if an effect perishes without effort, nevertheless, because it is a cause of pleasure, dispassion toward it does not arise. To this it is replied:
There is no happiness in what has passed, nor does it exist in what is not yet attained; even that which is present passes away—of what, indeed, is this toil yours?

First, there is no pleasure in past consciousness because it has already ceased; nor is there pleasure in future consciousness because it has not yet been attained; nor is there pleasure in present consciousness because it lacks duration. Since pleasure does not exist in this way, and thus there is no benefit derived from it, for what purpose would this exertion of yours in acquiring the karma that causes pleasure be undertaken by one who longs for the enjoyment of pleasure? The intended meaning is that the toil and effort involved in acquiring the causes of pleasure are entirely fruitless in every respect.

It is like the building of a house on a riverbank. Someone built a house on a riverbank, but that spot eroded; then he built it on another part of the bank, and that too eroded. In this way, an endless cycle occurred. Thus, for that builder of the house, there was great labor, yet no attainment of the fruit of his labor. Such is the nature of all worldly activities. And regarding this, it is said:
"For whose sake do you accumulate karmas, given that the movement of moments of consciousness is as fleeting as lightning?"
Because, when examined throughout the three periods of time, pleasure does not exist.
To this, he says: "Even if this is so, nevertheless, for the sake of the happiness of heaven, wholesome karma must certainly be performed. It is replied:
Even heaven would be terrifying to the wise, as it is equal to hell;
for them, existence—which is not terrifying—is in every respect difficult to find.
In that regard, because it is a gateway for various forms of affliction, because it is inflamed by the fire of afflictions produced by extremely intense sense objects,
and because of the abundance of delusion, the wise avoid even heaven as if it were hell, owing to its terrifying nature.

And therefore, for those who do not feel attachment even toward the riches of heaven—which are delightful due to the enjoyment of unimpeachable pleasures—how could they find delight in any other existence, which is like a cremation ground? Furthermore, the word "api" (even) here should be understood as displaced in order, and placed immediately after the word "svarga" (heaven). One should explain it thus: "Let alone any other existence; even heaven is equal to hell for the wise.
This is like the story of the release of the child from bondage. For example, there was once a king named Bāla.

He is of a cruel nature and possesses sharp iron-like punishments. Whoever is cast into his prison is bound tightly with five bonds upon the hands, feet, and neck. When he manages to liberate someone by some means, he then issues an order to the guards: "This man must be released from all bonds; however, he must be kept strictly guarded in whatever posture he desires until the end of his life.
Saying, "So be it," they surely carry out the king's command upon their heads. In that regard, whoever...

One who is released from the imprisonment of a child-king finds that even his liberation is as terrifying as the bondage itself, due to the particularity of the suffering involved. Likewise, for other great souls, existence is equal to hell; what other state of existence could there be that is not terrifying? Just as Bali was bound after having bestowed sovereignty over all the worlds—does he appear liberated by having given something else? Similarly, for those for whom even heaven is equal to hell because it is a cause of suffering, what other state of existence could there be that would not be terrifying?

Moreover, just as the wise, who are skilled in contemplating the defects of saṃsāra, perceive saṃsāra exactly as it is—entirely miserable and enveloped by the blazing flames of suffering—in that very same way:
If even a child were to fully understand the suffering of saṃsāra in every respect,
he would perish utterly at that very moment along with his mind.

If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) were able to perceive directly that suffering through which the Noble Ones (*ārya*) tremble with fear of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), their heart would shatter into a hundred pieces at that very moment. However, due to a lack of such realization, this person takes delight in *saṃsāra*. For the Noble Ones, however, the suffering of *saṃsāra*—held fast by the fortitude of their intent to benefit sentient beings through gratitude and great compassion—is not a cause for such terror; thus, it is impossible to conceive of their ultimate destruction.
The ordinary person, on the other hand, follows the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Because of the deficiency in the cultivation of its antidote, [the body] would certainly disintegrate into atoms if one were to fully understand the suffering of *saṃsāra* in every respect—just like one struck by a *yakṣa*, or like a foolish leader. For example, someone was struck by a *yakṣa*, yet he did not see that *yakṣa*. He thought to himself: "As long as that *yakṣa* is unseen, such suffering has arisen; if he were seen, then my body would fall apart like a handful of chaff.
And it is just as with a foolish leader who, out of greed for sovereignty, lives...

Having abandoned the state of a householder, he takes up leadership once again. Thus, if even a fool were to realize the suffering of saṃsāra, he would, out of fear of that, undergo absolute destruction through the renunciation of all existence; this is the meaning of liberation. And it is said in this regard:
"If a fool were to understand the fruit of evil exactly as the Buddhas know it to be, he would become a Victor (Jina) at that very moment."
Moreover, in cyclic existence, happiness would belong to one who possesses the capacity for actions and who exerts effort; yet, upon investigation, such a person is not found.
One who is free from pride is rare;
one who possesses pride is not endowed with compassion.
Thus it has been said that he who is the light of lights, the supreme refuge, is exceedingly difficult to find.

For one who is capable, pride necessarily arises from the acquisition of objects to be experienced as pleasure through human effort in various activities, and from the protection of what has been acquired. Through this pride, imagining himself to be superior and unable to tolerate others' excellence, he becomes merciless in his desire to strike them down. And for such a merciless person, there is only the culmination in the states of woe.

Where, then, could there be prosperity for him from which the experience of happiness might be expected? For this very reason, the Blessed One said that a person who is "light unto light" is rare, because one who is possessed by pride born of lineage, wealth, power, or birth is certain to fall downward, as was the case with the son of Jamadagni. Just as the son of Jamadagni, though capable, made the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times due to his pride and lack of compassion; therefore, one who is both capable and free from pride is extremely rare, and even rarer still is one who is proud yet endowed with compassion. Since this is so—
The Blessed One said: "Light is difficult to find; light is the supreme goal.

If this is so, then those who possess pride (māna) are censurable because their evil conduct leads to ruin; conversely, those who are free from pride are praiseworthy because they practice the Dharma, which is the means for attaining the happiness of heaven. Consequently, saṃsāra is not categorically censured by them. To this it is replied: attachment even to the Dharma is improper due to its potential for perversion. For instance:

In this world, it is said that even for one who has withdrawn from sense objects, an object of experience is obtained through some cause; thus, dharma is remembered as being even contrary [to worldly expectations].

It is said that he who is indifferent toward sense objects abandons them by undertaking the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Yet, when such a person dies here and is reborn in a royal family or in the heavens, if he is then embraced by that world [of sense pleasure], attachment to this [state] is not superior;

it is like a ram intended for slaughter. Just as one wishing to strike a ram does not turn back even from afar, so too is the seeker of sense objects who has not turned away from them. Thus, for these reasons, such a "dharma" should be abandoned because it is contrary [to true liberation].
Furthermore, even that sovereignty which is the fruit of dharma should not be relied upon by the wise, because it lacks true mastery and because it is a locus for various calamities; for instance:
Sovereignty is the fruit of merit, and that must always be guarded against others;
for how can that which must always be guarded from others truly be one's own?

For sovereignty is the fruit of previously performed karma, and that is designated as "one's own. Yet, it must be constantly guarded here against adversaries. If it were truly one's own, it would not need to be guarded against adversaries at all. And how can that which requires a continuous application of protective measures because it can be seized by others be called "one's own"? Thus, this person, preoccupied with the constant application of protection and utterly exhausted, when indeed will he ever taste the flavor of the sense objects? Therefore, even its fruit is not sufficient for his benefit.

Like a teacher: just as a teacher is always to be saluted and one must always remain vigilant toward him, so too must that sovereignty—which is produced by the power of merit—be constantly protected from kings and others. And how can that which must be protected at all times be considered one's own? Furthermore, because worldly dharma is unstable, placing reliance upon it is not superior. For indeed: whatever the state of the world may be, dharma conforms to each of those states;
therefore, the world appears as if more powerful than even dharma.

For whatever established practice the world ordains—such as the giving away of a daughter or the taking of a wife according to the conventions of region, family, and lineage—the Dharma conforms to each of those; for it is well known that "Dharma" is the name for each such established practice. And this principle is not logical for something established by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), insofar as it would become otherwise due to the difference in place and time. Therefore, it is not appropriate to have excessive regard for this [conventional Dharma].

It is like the marriage of a daughter. A certain man, having gone among the Yavanas, saw a Yavana who, having kindled a fire, was causing sound to issue from that fire by means of a magical spell (*vidyā*), saying, "The daughter is offered as a wife for you. That man was one whose conduct was dominated by extreme passion, and the daughter was beautiful in her own land.

A young woman remained there. Then, that man requested the spell from the Yavana with great effort and by offering wealth. Having returned to his own country, desiring to take his daughter as his wife, he wished to have the matter proclaimed before the fire. Agni said to him, "The established custom of this country is otherwise. Thus, even over against dharma, worldly convention is more powerful.

Here it is argued: there is no experience of pleasant sensation without the arising of desired objects; and since that arising of objects occurs only for those who have performed meritorious deeds, therefore Dharma must certainly be practiced by one who seeks such objects. To this, it is replied:
An object is desired because it is pure, yet that very same object becomes loathsome;
for one who finds excellence in its renunciation, what is the use of even having accomplished it?

This object here, consisting of the five desired qualities of sensory pleasure and designated as form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, is obtained through wholesome karma; yet for those beings who desire liberation, it is loathsome—like a dog with its body smeared with impurities—and its renunciation is superior because it is the root of misfortune, being impermanent and impure.

Since it does not bring about liberation by its very nature, since it gives rise to afflictions such as passion, and since it is a basis for negligence, there is no purpose whatsoever even when it is accomplished; thus, the exertion in acquiring the qualities that result from sense objects is entirely in vain. Therefore, attachment should be abandoned toward dharma just as it is toward adharma.

It is like the case of the alms-gathering monk from Kamboja. A certain monk went for alms in the country of Kamboja. He was told by a certain deceitful person acting for his own sake: "Do not say anything here for the time being; while wandering for alms, you will become an object of ridicule. This [is] in this...

This was the limit [of his deception]. Because Arjuna was full of faith, he acted accordingly. Then that group of people realized: "This machine was made by a man who competes with us and sent to us. They exclaimed, "Oh! His opening and closing of the eyes and so forth have been made to appear just like those of a human being! Thus they described every single limb. Thereupon, they too made similar machines and sent them to that man.

Then that man said to the monk, "Now speak the words 'from the cessation of that'. He did so, and the words "health and so forth" were uttered. Thereupon, they were filled with amazement and said, "This is impossible for us; we have been defeated by him. That rogue who merely resembles a monk becomes truly contemptible once his true nature is recognized; such is this case as well.

Here it is argued: "Even though the dharma that takes the object as its means is purposeless because the object itself is contemptible, nevertheless, since kingdoms are heavy with the pleasure of tasting the flavor of command, a king should exert himself toward sovereign powers for that sake. To this it is said: For indeed, it is not possible for everyone to have their work accomplished by means of a command; and therefore—
The dharma of one who has no task to accomplish by means of a command is useless;
for he whose desired object cannot be accomplished otherwise [is the one who must act].
Chapter VIII.
Pārikarmika I and likewise for whom?

The king’s son was exceedingly dear to him; once, having risen up in revolt, he was defeated and captured by that king in battle. Because that king perceived his faults, his affection for him vanished. Thus, in one who recognizes faults, passion does not abide toward anything. Not only is there no passion for a long time due to seeing all faults, but its abandonment is also possible for this further reason: because of the absence of any objective basis for passion. Demonstrating this, he says:
In that very same thing someone becomes attached, in that very same thing someone becomes repelled, and in that very same thing someone becomes deluded; therefore, desire is meaningless.

For passion arises dependent upon an object that causes attachment, yet that object which causes attachment is not established by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). For that very thing which is an object of attachment for one person is perceived as an object of aversion or delusion for another. If an object causing attachment existed by way of its own intrinsic nature, it would always be so for everyone; however, no such rule is observed. For instance, while one person feels passion toward a certain thing, another feels aversion toward that very same thing, and yet another feels deluded regarding it. Therefore, desire for sense objects is empty because it is not established by way of its own intrinsic nature.

It is not the case that the abandonment of passion is impossible for a yogi who is intent on meditating on the emptiness of attractive objects; rather, the abandonment of passion certainly exists, as in the case of [the three views of] mother, wife, and slave-girl. Suppose a certain man has two wives: one stays with their son, while the second stays without her son. When that mother sees her own son, she becomes joyful; seeing him, the co-wife becomes distressed; but the slave-girl, having seen him, remains indifferent. Thus, there is no establishment of the intrinsic nature of the objective support for passion and the other afflictions.

Having thus established the non-existence of passion and the like through the non-establishment of their objective support (ālambana), he now says the following, desiring to establish the non-existence of passion and the like also through the non-establishment of their cause (hetu).
Without conceptual construction, the existence of passion and the like is not found;
what intelligent person would grasp both the ultimate reality and conceptual construction?

"Passion, hatred, and delusion are said to have their origin in conceptual construction" (MMK 23.1ab). According to this statement, improper conceptualization regarding sense objects is the cause for the establishment of passion and the rest. Consequently, since those things certainly exist only when conceptual construction is present, it is determined that they lack intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), like a snake imagined upon a coiled rope. Furthermore, whoever accepts the intrinsic establishment of passion and the rest must necessarily not accept that their birth depends upon conceptual construction, as that would contradict their having an intrinsic nature.

For if that object is real, why would its existence depend upon conceptual construction? And if it does depend [upon it], how can it be a real object? Thus, because their mental continuums are illuminated by the light of scripture supported by reasoning, the wise do not accept that what is established in its own nature is produced by conceptual construction; the dull-witted, however, proceed in some manner due to error, such as [the case of] a skull from the head of a meditator.

...as follows: A certain meditator had fallen into a mental delusion, thinking, "A skull is stuck to my head. Someone else dropped another skull [onto his head], saying, "This has fallen upon your head. Having understood it to be so, he became composed, because of the disappearance of that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). To this, [the opponent] says: The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions] certainly exists, because they constitute bondage. For instance, a woman, bound by passion directed toward a man, does not pass beyond him; and a man, [bound] by passion directed toward a woman...
"It is said that one who is bound with a woman does not abandon her. To this it is replied:
"For anyone, there exists no such thing as being bound to another."

For just as passion (*rāga*) is not established by way of its own nature because its arising depends upon conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), so too, since the essential natures of woman and man are unestablished, there is no bondage by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between any object and any other object. Thus, passion is not established by way of its own nature simply because it is the cause of bondage. Even if one were to set aside this analysis and imagine that one person is bound to another, even so: [it remains untenable].
The separation of one who is bound from another is not logical.

For if the other [the object] were by its own nature the cause of bondage, then because there would be no alteration of that nature, liberation would be impossible. "Separation," "liberation," and "emancipation" are synonymous. Since liberation does exist, the other cannot be the cause of bondage by way of its own nature. And since there is no cause of bondage, from where could bondage arise? Thus, one can maintain that passion and the rest are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), and are abandoned through the vision of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. This is like the joining of a black and a white ox.

It is like this: just as a black ox is not for the yoking of a white one, nor is a white ox for the yoking of a black one, but rather for the hole of the yoke; so too, the sense faculties are not for the sake of the objects, nor are the objects for the sake of the sense faculties, but rather the desire and passion (*chanda-rāga*) that exist therein is the bondage.

If afflictions (*kleśa*) are turned back through such investigation, why is it that those who have not conquered their afflictions are generally seen? It is because they lack faith and resolve (*adhimukti*) in the profound Dharma. For instance:
In this Dharma, even doubt does not arise for one of little merit;
yet by mere doubt, existence becomes worn out and shattered.

For an ignorant person, whose vision has been habituated to error throughout beginningless saṃsāra, is attached to things that are like reflections as being "this is real. Because his mental continuum lacks the roots of virtue that serve as the cause for conviction in emptiness, he regards the teaching on the emptiness of intrinsic nature as if it were a precipice. For such a being, regarding this dharma of emptiness, not even the doubt "Is it thus, or is it not? arises, except for a contrary certainty. Consequently, since the cause of liberation is perverted, how could there be liberation for him?

If, however, for some reason, while the teaching of the dharma of emptiness is being given, one should give rise to doubt—thinking, "Is this dharma thus, or is it not thus?"—then by this mere doubt, his saṃsāra will certainly become utterly shattered. For when he takes hold of the thought "it is thus," that very process leads to the destruction of the thieves of the afflictions (kleśas).
