Alternatively, one who is in doubt but seeks certainty becomes firmly established in right view through the power of scripture supported by reasoning; thus, for the sake of the destruction of the afflictions, he will bring about the cessation of saṃsāra. Even at the time of doubt, his saṃsāra is seen to be already shattered, because he abides in a state conducive to its dissolution, just like the royal horse Bālāha when seized by a rākṣasī and subsequently liberated.

Just as the caravan leader, whose vehicle was broken and who had been seized by a rākṣasī, was being treated as her husband and was forbidden from going toward the southern direction—being told, "You must never go to the southern direction"—he, wondering why she was restraining him, went there; having encountered Bālāhaka, the king of horses, he was released from that rākṣasī and reached the far shore of the ocean. If he had not had that doubt, he would not have been separated from that rākṣasī, nor would he have reached the far shore of the ocean.

Furthermore, regarding this dharma characterized by the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), even a doubt concerning it leads to the disintegration of cyclic existence (*bhava*); for that [doubt], the Blessed One has described non-decline and growth from the first moment of patience (*kṣānti*) until liberation. But such is not the case with worldly dharmas; for they are exhausted through the exhaustion of their maturation (*vipāka*), and they do not proceed even due to the deficiency of conditions. Indeed, [this is not so] for the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

The Teacher said that the perfections, such as generosity and the rest, when presided over by those [insights], become capable of reaching the city of omniscience, like those who are blind from birth; thus it is so.
He who has no devotion for that Dharma whose increase until liberation the Sage has proclaimed— clearly, he is not wise.

For he who does not produce devotion toward the Dharma—which is the ultimate benefactor and possesses the highest excellence—is a fool who, by perceiving danger where there is safety, merely reveals his own stupidity. Therefore, thinking "May such stupidity not be mine," the wise should cultivate devotion toward the vision of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

It is like sugar-candied sweets (*śarkarāmodaka*) and like a sealing-stick (*śalākāmudrā*). Just as sugar-candied sweets are to be tasted from all sides, so it is [with this teaching]. It is like a certain man who has mastered two spells (*vidyā*): by reciting one over a sealing-stick, he effects the pacification of all diseases; and by applying the second as a seal, he does the same. Then, he says to a friend: "Take these two spells; they will be of benefit to you. But the friend does not take them. Later, when that friend has died, a great disease arises in him. He...
He was incurable and died because of that very [condition].
Now, are these entities (*padārtha*) actually non-empty, yet perceived as empty for the sake of detachment (*vairāgya*), or are they designated as empty by their very nature? It is said in reply:
That which is not empty is not seen as empty; may there be nirvāṇa for me.
For what reason? Because the Tathāgatas do not describe nirvāṇa as resulting from wrong view.

The perception of a thing as otherwise than it actually exists is false perception (*mithyādarśana*). If, while things were non-empty by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they were perceived as empty of intrinsic nature, then the attainment of *nirvāṇa* would result from false perception alone. However, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not establish the attainment of *nirvāṇa* for a person of false view, because they establish the attainment of *nirvāṇa* only through one who is preceded by right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

And therefore, because they are dependently originated like an illusion, entities, while being empty of intrinsic nature, are realized as empty by their very nature by the Noble Ones—whose mental continuums are purified by the vision of the reality of things as they truly exist, and who are untainted by the stains of conceptualizing the extremes of imputation and denial.
It is like the case of the *vellaka* at night; a certain *vellaka* was sent by his teacher...

At night, [the novice] was frequently sent for the purpose of fetching drink. Then, on one occasion, he was told by him: "This is not permissible for monks; how is it that you drink? He replied, "It is water. On another day, he brought only water. He said, "Why has something else been brought like this? The śrāmaṇera said, "Since you drink it thinking it is simply water, what difference is there in this case?"

If indeed all things are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for what purpose is the sequential arising of the world of sentient beings and the receptacle-world (*sattvabhājanaloka*) taught as proceeding through ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth? Is it not the case that, since intrinsic nature is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), one should teach only the emptiness of intrinsic nature? This is not so. For it is not possible to demonstrate the reality characterized by the emptiness of intrinsic nature without first teaching the worldly process of arising. Therefore, the teaching on arising must also be given, because it serves as a staircase for entering into reality.

For the sake of attaining the bliss of cessation through the relinquishment of all attachments, even the teaching on the emptiness of intrinsic nature must be given; this is so within this, the Tathāgata’s dispensation.
Where worldly activity prevails, there the discourse on the conventional is described;
where cessation prevails, there the discourse on the ultimate truth is described.

Wherein the process of the progression of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)—beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and so forth—is taught in sequence for the sake of destroying the notions of causelessness, a single cause, or discordant causes, by means of the conceptualization of the reality of specific and general characteristics; there, it should be understood by the wise that "progression" is described. However, where the non-arising nature and the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are taught, there the cessation of the progression of cyclic existence is described. [This is] because of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Because of the realization of the ultimate truth of non-duality, one who is unattached to everything and free from craving for sensations brings about the cessation of birth, old age, death, and so forth, by means of the cessation of the causes beginning with grasping (*upādāna*), which is conditioned by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

This is like entering a hole: just as when entering a hole, whatever activity of equipment there may be must all be abandoned, as no purpose whatsoever is served by it; likewise, all worldly activities, being devoid of essence, must be relinquished by the wise. For [it is said] that "activity is a dharma.
If this is so—

"In the discourse on ultimate truth, nothing exists because all phenomena are empty; therefore, the consequence follows that everything is non-existent. And because of this total non-existence, nothing would need to be done, since agent, object, action, and so forth would be entirely absent. Furthermore, due to the absence of action and the rest, there would be no liberation; thus, everything is untenable. To this, it is replied:
"What shall I do? Everything is unreal"—from this thought fear arises in you.
If there were something actually to be done, this Dharma would not be a means of cessation.

For it is precisely because everything is non-existent that this ultimate reality (paramārtha-dharma) is logically capable of causing engagement and withdrawal. Why, then, would one seeking cessation not strive for the total absence [of things], which provides no basis for action and so forth? If, indeed, even in this [state of non-existence] there were something to be done, just as in the case of engagement, then since the object—which is the fruit of the action—would also be engaged with, that very thing would be an engagement; how, then, could this dharma lead to Nirvana?
It is like a mirage. For just as a mirage produces the perception of water but that water does not exist, so too is the notion of a self regarding the aggregates (*skandha*).

Since there is no action whatsoever in a phenomenon that brings about cessation, the position of emptiness is superior. He rebukes one who is attached to the path of emptiness and finds fault with the contrary position of intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvapakṣa*).
Attachment exists toward your own side, while the opposing side is unpleasant to you;
you who move in duality will not attain Nirvana, nor the auspicious state.

In brief, there are two kinds of positions: one’s own position and the position of another. In this regard, if you have attachment toward your own position and consider the position of emptiness to be superior—regarding the position of another as false and thus disagreeable—you will not go to nirvāṇa. For there is no nirvāṇa for one who is struck down by attraction and aversion and who dwells in duality. Indeed, those who are indifferent toward everything attain the auspicious state, which has the singular flavor of the bliss of non-decline through the severing of attachments.

It is like the case of the student Baṭu and the teacher Saṃghasena. A certain student was desirous of hearing a treatise from the teacher Saṃghasena. On one occasion, he was told by him, "Become a lay follower (*upāsaka*). On another day, he said to that teacher, "Teacher, I have become a lay follower. For what reason? [He replied,] "Because, upon seeing the brahmins, I wish to have them killed. To this, he said: "Even if..."

Nirvāṇa is supreme bliss because it is free from all afflictions; nevertheless, it is impossible to attain, because the means for its attainment are exceedingly difficult to perform. As for cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), however, since it is accomplished without effort and is therefore easily attained, we are inclined toward it. To this, it is replied: you have understood the matter perversely. Why? Because: "For one who does not act, there is nirvāṇa; for one who acts, there is rebirth.
Therefore, nirvāṇa is to be attained with ease by one who is free from anxiety, but the other [rebirth] is not."

Nirvana is attained by one who is free from mental concern and whose activity regarding wholesome and other deeds has been relinquished; therefore, Nirvana is easily reached. However, because it is accomplished through the engagement in wholesome and unwholesome actions, rebirth—being the opposite of Nirvana—is not easily attained. It is not fitting for a wise person to reject Nirvana, which is obtained without effort, and instead to desire rebirth, which is obtained only through the exhaustion of various activities.

It is like the means for achieving health and strength. For many conditions are seen that serve as the means for achieving strength for one who is healthy; yet when one does not desire even the slightest distinction, then one becomes indifferent to all such conditions. If, indeed, Nirvana belongs to one who does nothing at all, then for what purpose is the exposition of the meaning of impermanence and so forth performed here in this treatise? It is said: [it is] for the sake of causing the world, which is consumed by cyclic existence (saṃsāra), to become weary of cyclic existence. For it is thus:
For one who has no sense of revulsion toward this world, how can there be devotion to Śiva?
And escaping from this worldly existence is as difficult as leaving one's own home.

One whose mind is distressed by *saṃsāra* resorts to *nirvāṇa* for the sake of escaping it; but how could one who lacks such distress seek it? Precisely because of this absence of distress, those of small intellect do not venture to depart from existence (*bhava*). It is just as one cannot abandon one's own home—even if it possesses little substance—because it is difficult to sever one's attachments to it; such is this [existence].

It is like the case of a condemned man who begs for a drink. Suppose a certain person condemned to death has been cast out for execution and must be killed immediately; yet he begs for a drink. In this same way, even for those in the world, their desire is not fulfilled.

Rather, let the wealthy not abandon their homes—which are easily obtained through the enjoyment of sensual pleasures—lest they, by virtue of that wealth, go toward Nirvana. However, for those for whom it is impossible to remedy the causes of suffering such as disease, poverty, and so forth, the renunciation of saṃsāra is indeed appropriate. For instance:
Some are seen overcome by suffering, longing for death;
yet, due solely to delusion, they do not then attain the supreme state.

Some, afflicted by the suffering of disease and separation, cast aside self-attachment and even throw themselves from a precipice; likewise, if they were to discern cyclic existence as suffering and utterly uproot self-attachment, they would remain not far from the bliss of nirvāṇa. But those whose vision is perverted do not act in this way due to delusion, and thus they do not attain nirvāṇa.

It is like one who has drunk gruel and gone to sleep, or like one who is hesitant about drinking medicine. Someone, having drunk gruel, fell asleep and subsequently became even more miserable. Likewise, the more fools desire happiness, the more they become utterly miserable. Just as someone, thinking "I shall drink medicine," becomes oily (upasnigdha), yet due to that oiliness becomes hesitant—wondering whether the medicine should be drunk or what exactly should be drunk—and thus is not freed from his illness;
so too all foolish ordinary people (*bālapṛthagjana*) are characterized by an attachment to the afflictions of suffering.

Even those whose afflictions have been liquefied, yet who—out of uncertainty regarding the drinking of the medicine of dispassion—are unable to destroy the disease of ignorance, do not attain the supreme state through liberation from the disease of all afflictions because they have not drunk the medicine of the afflictions.

Regarding this, it is asked: "If this is so, and since Nirvana alone should be sought by the total renunciation [of everything], let there be only discourse on meditation for its attainment. For what purpose, then, did the Blessed One also provide discourse on generosity and ethical discipline? It is said in reply: "The realm of sentient beings is indeed threefold, distinguished as inferior, middling, and superior. It is for the sake of these distinctions that the Blessed One’s teaching possesses such variety."
The object to be enjoined (vidheya) is that which follows this [syāt].

It is like a young child; just as a young child cannot be awakened by any other language, so too is the world of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). For this very reason, the Blessed One taught doctrines such as existence and non-existence as skillful means for leading the world [to liberation].
It is described as existent, non-existent, both existent and non-existent, and neither.

"Existence" (*sat*) was taught to wash away the stain of perceiving the non-existence of all things; "non-existence" (*asat*) was taught to abandon attachment to existence; "both existence and non-existence" (*sadasat*) was proclaimed to relinquish the perception of both modes; and "neither" (*nobhaya*) was revealed to sever the proliferation of all conceptual forms (*prapañca*). Furthermore, you yourself should first reflect:
is it not the case that by the power of a disease, even medicine becomes what is called "wholesome"?
Diseases are to be counteracted; and because of the diversity of their causes, there are many medicines, and not just one that is applicable in every case. Such is this [teaching].

It is like the giving of Dharma-water to a yakṣa, a preta, and a renunciant; and it is like the vision of a yakṣa standing before one. For example, there were three brothers: among them, one had gone forth as a renunciant, the second had become a yakṣa possessed of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), and the third was born as a preta with a mouth of firebrands. Both of them went into the presence of that bhikṣu. Then, for the purpose of making the yakṣa aware of the cause of his pride, that bhikṣu exposed the fault of his immoral conduct (*dauḥśīlya*). [The sentence or paragraph continues on the following page.]

By the offering of water to a preta, one pacifies its unbearable suffering caused by fire; furthermore, in order to make known the cause of that suffering, the fault of stinginess is made known. Thus, due to the diversity of the dispositions of sentient beings, there is a diversity in the teaching of the Dharma. For example, suppose someone’s father has requested a daughter from another region, and that father has passed away. His mother says to him: "Go to see that girl; a yakṣa who was your father’s friend, named so-and-so, is there—ask for her from him. He does so. Then that yakṣa [leads him] to a celestial palace...

Having seized him by means of this [power], he departed into the air. A man was approaching, and that yakṣa said to his son, "Go and terrify him. The son did so; having returned, he asked him, "For what reason was this man terrified? He replied, "This is a renunciant; I cannot endure his splendor. Then, having led him to the city, the yakṣa placed his son in a secluded spot and entered the city himself to search for a maiden.

And when that yakṣa saw the girl, passion arose within him; he seized her. Meanwhile, the son went there himself, wondering what his father had been doing for so long, and upon seeing her seized by him, he entreated him: "Release this girl; she shall be your daughter-in-law. In the same way, the teaching of the Dharma is to be understood.

Because these teachings on existence, non-existence, and so forth, are directed toward internal reflection, that which is neither of these two [extremes] is the teaching of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). And regarding that ultimate truth:
For one with right view, there is a supreme state; for one who has seen [the truth], there is an auspicious destiny.
Therefore, the wise should always apply their minds to the contemplation of the inner self.

Indeed, O one of right view, by means of knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*), the supreme state—nirvāṇa—is attained when the ultimate truth is fully seen. When it is seen only slightly, a favorable rebirth among gods or humans occurs. Since nirvāṇa is attained through the complete vision of knowledge, whereas a favorable rebirth is attained when it is incomplete, a wise person should always apply their intellect to the contemplation of the internal self.
It is like the invitation to an unrighteous thief by a wealthy family. A certain thief used to go frequently to a monastery. He was told by a certain monk, "Please accept this gift for us. He...

He asked, "What kind of gift? The monk said, "Take the gift of the Dharma: the precepts. He replied, "I am unable to abstain from taking life, taking what is not given, and lying; however, I shall refrain from sexual misconduct. Having refrained from those [other acts], he entered the royal palace for the purpose of theft. There, he was invited by means of unrighteous conduct, but he did not desire it; and that matter was discovered by the king.
Therefore, a woman adorned with every ornament was bestowed upon him and he was honored. In this very way, within this internal reflection, the certain fruit is established as nirvāṇa;
yet, due to some deficiency of conditions, it might not be so.

In this case, even if one who knows reality does not attain nirvāṇa [in this life], he will certainly obtain it without effort in a future birth, just like [the ripening of] karma. Even if one devoted to the vision of reality in this life does not reach the culmination of dispassion (*virāga*), due to the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the knowledge of ultimate truth, he will necessarily obtain nirvāṇa without effort in a future birth, just like karma. For example, although the fruit of a fixed karma performed here may not manifest in this very life, its result is nonetheless certain.

The fruit arises in a subsequent birth, like the eating and planting of a mango tree. For one who, having eaten a mango, plants the seed without destroying it, although he does not obtain the fruit immediately resulting from the tasting of the seed, he nevertheless obtains great benefit after some time.
If this is so, and the knowledge of reality exists, for what reason are those liberated not seen? Indeed, some are even seen. Furthermore:
The successful accomplishment of all undertakings, when contemplated, is extremely difficult to find;
yet it is not that nirvana does not exist here, for those who are disciplined and liberated are rare.

Not only is dispassion (*virāga*) difficult to perceive, but indeed all undertakings have results that are hard to master. For thought alone does not accomplish the fruit; rather, it is the completeness of causes and conditions (*hetupratyayasāmagrī*) that brings about the desired result. And that completeness of causes and conditions is difficult to find. Therefore, in this world, the accomplishment of any task through mere thought is extremely rare. Likewise, although there is *nirvāṇa* in this teaching, because of the absence of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and the lack of internal correct discernment (*yoniśo vikalpa*), those who are disciplined are very difficult to find.

Because even those who are liberated from that [state] are difficult to find; therefore, one cannot conclude from the non-perception of liberation that there is an absence of the vision of reality, just as in the case of licking the plowshare of a *caṇḍālī*. For example, when a *caṇḍālī* is accused of theft, even though she is free from that fault, she does not venture to lick the plowshare, thinking: "How can I, being of an impure nature due to my status as a *caṇḍālī*, lick the plowshare in the presence of the gods? If she were to do so, she would be released from the accusation. In the same way, some fools, considering themselves inferior, do not venture toward Buddhahood.
To bring about [the attainment of Buddhahood].

If, moreover, they were to attain it through the proper method, they would certainly obtain Buddhahood. But how can it be ascertained that there is an end to this mass of afflictions (*kleśa*) that has been active for such a long time? It is said:
Having heard of the defects of the body, passion does not remain for even a moment.
By that very same path, surely the destruction of everything is attained.
Just as here, although this body has been protected with a sense of "mine" for a long time and pampered with various enjoyments, [it will eventually perish].

When a wise person hears of the lack of virtue in one who is subject to destruction and ungrateful, passion does not arise in them at that very moment. Likewise, when detachment is produced by that same path through thorough cultivation, is it not the case that even passion which has persisted for a long time is entirely and utterly destroyed? Consequently, liberation results from the severing of the bonds of passion without remainder, through seeing the worthlessness of all things—both external and internal—due to their emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), just as Cāṇakya abandoned the gold. Śa...

"Can I, by this means, produce even much gold?"—in this way, the practitioner of yoga (yogācāra), seeing that passion does not persist for even a moment merely upon hearing of the body's worthlessness, practices that very path [thinking]: "I am able, by this means and by this path, to effect the absolute cessation of passion.
To this, he asks: "How will there be an end to this continuum of births which has proceeded from beginningless time? It is said in reply:
Just as the end of a seed is seen, yet its beginning is not found,
so too, due to the deficiency of causes, there is no possibility of birth.

Just as the end of this seed-continuum—which has proceeded for a long time through a succession of causes and effects and is beginningless—is seen [to occur] due to the destruction by fire, so too there is no further arising of the birth from the seeds of consciousness, which, though beginningless, proceeds from causes in succession since beginningless time, because of the deficiency of its causes.
For it is karma, in dependence upon the afflictions (*kleśa*), that is capable of projecting birth; and those afflictions [are overcome] by knowledge.

Having reached non-existence due to contact with heat, this action is now incapable of projecting a birth because of the absence of its auxiliary conditions; thus, having completed its birth, it becomes cooled.

It is like a lamp, like parched sesame seeds, like a sky-wandering mendicant, and like a tree. Just as a lamp does not persist when its conditions are absent but persists when they are present; just as parched sesame seeds do not sprout; and just as a sky-wandering mendicant, having mastered the mineral *manaḥśilā*, used to travel through the air by means of it, but when that [power] was stolen away from him by another person through a spell...

Because of the absence of a cause, he has fallen away. Just as a tree does not grow again after its root is uprooted due to the absence of a cause, so too, because of the absence of the cause that is the adherence to existence (*bhāvābhiniveśa*), there is no arising of afflictions such as passion (*rāga*). Furthermore, the activity of Bodhisattvas does not proceed by the power of karma, but rather by the power of their vow (*praṇidhāna*). Therefore, it is most extremely difficult and most wonderful for a Bodhisattva that, while manifesting existence in all states of rebirth, he exerts himself for the sake of sentient beings and yet does not adhere to anything as a "sentient being."
And it has been said by the master Buddhapālita:
"Even though you perceive the world as empty, that you have been afflicted for so very long out of a desire to dispel the suffering of birth— that indeed is most wonderful!"
Thus it is said;
and he will demonstrate how that vision of the intrinsic nature of the entire world comes about through eight subsequent chapters.
In the *Catuḥśataka* on the Bodhisattva’s Yoga Practice by the Master Āryadeva, this is the eighth chapter, the Chapter on Preliminary Purification.
CHAPTER IX: REFUTATION OF THE MEANING OF ETERNITY (NITYĀRTHAPRATIṢEDHA) I

The teacher, wishing to begin the *Tattvaviniścaya* (Ascertainment of Reality) for the sake of his disciple— who has had the continuum of his mind washed by the water of the preceding chapters and is thus a fit vessel for the teaching of the nectar of reality— now speaks, demonstrating the worthlessness of the conditioned through its arising and passing away, so that the disciple may attain an understanding of the reality of things as they truly are by means of the remaining chapters.
Everything arises for the sake of some purpose; therefore, nothing exists eternally.

For activity in the world is indeed for the sake of a purpose, not something inherent; thus worldly people say, "This affection of his is produced by a specific cause, it is not inherent. Furthermore, since there is no arising of any single entity—whether it be the conditioned, the primary elements, the derivative matter, the mind, mental factors, the characterized, or the characteristics—it is, according to the circumstances, a collection (*kalāpa*).

It is the very arising of form (*rūpa*), because within that aggregate there exists a state of mutual cause and effect. That which, when present, something else comes to be, and in whose absence that other does not come to be—that is the cause, and the other is the effect. Since the other three elements do not exist without earth, and since they do exist when it is present, the production of earth arises for the sake of its specific function as an effect; thus, every conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*) has arisen for its own respective purpose as an effect.

And that which has arisen for the sake of a purpose is not eternal; for the word "eternal" (*nitya*) is a synonym for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), reality (*satya*), essence (*sāra*), substance (*vastu*), and entity (*dravya*). By the absence of these, it is understood that the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is without intrinsic nature, unreal, without essence, non-substantial, and a non-entity.

For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "The eye is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self; it is empty of that which is permanent, stable, eternal, and of an unchanging nature. Likewise, he said: "The eye is empty of the eye, by virtue of its being neither immutable nor indestructible. Why is that? Because its intrinsic nature (prakṛti) is such.
For this very reason, the Teacher declared: "Whatever is conditioned is of a deceptive and illusory nature."
And having ascertained that this statement is endowed with the reasoning to be set forth below, the Teacher said:
Therefore, apart from the Sage, there is no Tathāgata who exists as suchness.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, is a sage (*muni*) because of his union with the silence of the body, speech, and mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣya*). He alone is called the "Gone Thus" (*tathāgata*)—the Buddha who has gone in such a way—because he teaches the emptiness of the impermanent, [realizing] that the nature of phenomena is exactly as it is; not anyone else, because of their teaching of a perverted reality and their failure to fully awaken to the meaning of reality as it truly exists. As it has been said: "Just as past suchness is, so too is the present and the future."
All phenomena are seen as such; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
Thus [it is said].

Alternatively, this is another meaning: whatever possesses the nature of arising necessarily possesses the nature of cessation, because of the teaching that "old age and death have birth as their condition. Since for that which has arisen, its very purpose is destruction—for such is the purpose of arising—therefore everything that has arisen exists for the sake of a result; thus, it is not eternal.
Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist...
The meaning is "because. Since this is so, therefore, apart from the Sage (muni), there is no Tathāgata who exists in accordance with reality (*yathābhāva*).
The meaning of this is as before.

Alternatively, because there is no experience of the fruit of karma without those specific times, places, and states through which the three types of karma to be experienced as feelings are to be felt, all things—whether internal or external—arise for the sake of some purpose; they do not exist by way of their own intrinsic nature alone. Therefore, nothing is eternal. For if it were established by way of its own intrinsic nature, it would be eternal precisely because that intrinsic nature is indestructible; yet such is not the case.
Therefore, permanence does not exist;
the meaning is that everything is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And this emptiness has not been taught in the discourses of teachers other than the Tathāgata; thus he says:
"Therefore, apart from the Sage, there is no Tathāgata who exists as things truly are."
Thus it is said.

But the logicians (tārkika) explain as follows: "That which is accepted by another as unarisen for the sake of an effect is [in fact] arisen, because it has the purpose of an effect, just like something that has already arisen for the sake of an effect. To this we reply: first of all, the existence of those imagined atoms of earth and so forth—which are devoid of arising and ceasing—is [as non-existent] as a sky-flower and the like.

It is impossible [for that to] persist. Nor is it logical to establish impermanence by proving the production [of an effect] through superimposing causality upon things that do not exist, because the fact that [the cause] has the effect as its purpose is itself unestablished. Furthermore, if one were to accept a reason established only for the opponent, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Since the opponent must be prevented from accepting an untenable entity, it is not proper to accept that the permanent [cause] has the effect as its purpose. Moreover, it is not logical for this [proponent] to point out a contradiction with inference regarding the opponent's thesis, because such a contradiction must be pointed out only by means of what is established for both parties. This is also the case for one for whom [the reason] is established for both.

Since there is no possibility of sublation by inference, even by means of what is established for oneself, there is indeed no sublation by inference; surely, that too would simply be an inability to communicate the meaning. For a learned person does not take the trouble to explain a meaning that is easily understood with difficulty. Furthermore, because space is also declared to be a cause for the arising of the sprout of visual consciousness, and because it is mentioned among the six elements in the Sūtras, and because it serves as the basis for the designation of a "person" (pudgala), the state of being an effect would certainly be inconclusive.

If it is argued that space lacks the status of being a cause because of the principle that "a cause undergoing transformation becomes the cause of another," this is not so. For in that context, that by which something is produced is the cause; thus, a producer alone is intended as the cause, just as a seed is the cause of a sprout. However, space is indeed accepted as a cause in the sense of being a mere instrumental condition (*nimitta*). Otherwise, the lack of contradiction between the Sūtras and the Śāstras would not have been established.

It might be so; however, the Teacher does not establish impermanence by way of [mere] arising, because he maintains that all things are entirely without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This is because, in the subsequent section concerning reality (*tattva*), even that [arising] will be refuted just like permanence. For he will say:
"The simultaneous occurrence of arising, stability, and destruction is impossible;
their sequential occurrence is impossible; when, then, could their occurrence exist?"
Thus it is said in the treatise as well:
"If there is a grasping at the impermanent as permanent, that is indeed a perversion."
"Even the grasping that 'it is impermanent'—is this not a perversion regarding the empty?
Thus [it is said].

Moreover, since a real entity (*vastu*) is established by worldly consensus, the employment of inference for its establishment is entirely purposeless. Even one who, out of delusion, conceives of a non-entity as having the existence of a real entity can still be made to understand the intended meaning through what is commonly accepted by ordinary people. Furthermore, in the proof of the true nature of a real entity, even the three members of the syllogism (*avayavatraya*) are unestablished, just like the probandum itself; therefore, the [inferential] purpose is simply impossible.

Because of this [dependence on the means of proof], the effort of logicians in formulating logical reasoning appears entirely futile. For instance, even ordinary people who have not studied the definitions of logic are skilled in determining worldly matters; they comprehend an object exactly as it exists and communicate that same understanding to others.

Furthermore, since impermanence is well-known in the world, and since even the world recognizes it, it is impossible to claim that the Tathāgata alone is the speaker of non-erroneous meaning in that regard. However, as for the world which, having superposed its own conceptual characteristics, perceives impermanence—because it does not realize that the thing [itself] has the nature of being deceptive and illusory—it is logical to say that the Tathāgata alone is the one who sees without error in all cases.

Regarding this, some say: "It is true that what has arisen for the sake of a specific effect is not eternal; however, those entities that are deficient in both factors—such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth up to the mind (*manas*)—and those entities that are deficient in only one factor—such as the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of earth and so forth—will be eternal. Since their existence and eternality are not understood [by others], the Tathāgata is not one who sees things without error. To demonstrate the irrationality of their view, the Master says:
There is no existence without dependence.

Having perceived the existence of pleasure and so forth, which arise in dependence upon their respective causes and conditions, how could one not understand through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) that those things which are not dependently originated do not exist? Indeed, it is entirely appropriate for one to realize more clearly their non-existence, like that of a sky-lotus and the like. If one does not realize this, it is certainly observed that there is a distortion of vision caused by superimposition, as in the case of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). Therefore, there is no existence without dependence.
And this very principle is invariable everywhere with respect to any object that is differentiated by distinctions of time, substance, and place; thus he says:
"Sometimes, for someone, somewhere"—
since this is so.
Since nothing whatsoever exists anywhere at any time, therefore there is no eternal entity.

The first half [of this verse] is the conclusion regarding what has been established. Since, in this way, existence and permanence do not exist for those categories postulated by others because they are not dependently originated, it is thereby established that the Tathāgata possesses unerring vision; for he has known that which exists as existing—namely, that which is dependently originated—and that which does not exist as non-existing—namely, that which is postulated by others and is not dependently originated.
Furthermore, even those who claim that the Great One (mahat) and so forth [exist] merely through the manifestation and disappearance of creation and dissolution...

Those who, by means of mere manifestation through the concealment of their own non-existence, maintain the eternity [of the self], do not escape the aforementioned refutation, as they do not accept that anything arises dependently.

Now, it might be argued: pleasure and so forth are indeed dependently originated; and the self is their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Since it is not logical for that which is non-existent to be an inherent cause, the self must exist because its effects are perceived. Furthermore, this very self is eternal, because it exists and lacks a cause; for whatever exists and whose cause is not perceived is eternal.
"If the self exists, then things of that same nature will also exist.
To this it is said: Things of that same nature might exist if the self itself existed; however, it does not exist. How so? Because:
An entity does not exist without a cause.

"Entity," "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), and "self" (*ātman*) are synonyms; such a thing cannot possibly exist without a cause. For it has been accepted by the opponent himself that this [nature] is causeless, and it is established that what is devoid of a cause—like the horn of a donkey and so forth—does not exist. If it is argued that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) due to space (*ākāśa*) and other such things, we say no;
for their existence is likewise denied in the very same manner.
Now, if—out of a desire to avoid this fault—one were to accept that it possesses a cause even though that would contradict what has been previously asserted, even so its eternity would be lost;
for there exists no eternal thing that possesses a cause.
The intention is that [the self] is like pleasure and so forth because it possesses a cause; since this is the case.
Therefore, the knower of reality says that there is no accomplishment through causelessness, nor is there accomplishment [at all].
For it was said by the Blessed One:
"The wise person has conviction in dependent phenomena,
and does not take recourse in extreme views."
He understands that phenomena have causes and conditions;
there is no such thing as a phenomenon without cause or condition— this is the nature of reality.
Thus, because this teaching conforms to the logical proofs as they have been described, it is established that the Tathāgata alone is the knower of the non-perverted meaning.

Now, one might argue: "Since the impermanence of produced objects such as jars and pleasure is perceived, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the permanence of unproduced things such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth will follow. This too is incorrect; for if this were accepted, then having perceived the existence of produced things such as jars and pleasure, their opposite—the non-existence of unproduced things such as the self—would result by means of presumptive testimony. Demonstrating precisely this, he says:
If, having seen that what is produced is impermanent, one [concludes] that the unproduced is eternal;
then, having seen the existence of the produced, let it be that by that very fact the eternal does not exist.
Furthermore, that which does not exist cannot possess permanence, nor can an existing thing be impermanent.

Now, it might be argued: "Since space (*ākāśa*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*)—which are enumerated in the Abhidharma treatises—are unconditioned (*akṛtaka*) existents accepted as being eternal and existent, the demonstration that the unconditioned is non-existent is contradicted by what you yourself accept.
This too is not the case, because:
Ordinary people imagine space and the other [elements] to be eternal;
yet even by means of worldly [perception], the wise do not perceive any real objects within them.

Since the conventional designation "space" (ākāśa) applies solely to the mere absence of form (rūpa), there is no such thing as space that exists as a substantial entity. However, because there is no obstruction to the arising of material things when other forms are absent, that very absence of other forms is called "space" (ākāśa) because entities shine forth extensively within it. Thus, regarding this non-substantiality which is a mere nothingness, those deluded by the instruction of its mere name [have been misled] by the Abhidharma treatises...

Therefore, that substantiality (*vastutva*) which is superimposed by the Vaibhāṣikas is not a valid means of cognition; thus, it is not logical for them to challenge our position by alleging that it contradicts our own assertions. For instance, those who are experts in the intrinsic nature of things do not perceive, even through ordinary worldly cognition, any denotable essence whatsoever when the term "space" is employed, in the way that they perceive solidity and so forth when the terms "earth" and the like are employed.

How much less, then, could those established in the knowledge of the intrinsic nature of things perceive the essential form of that [space], while not perceiving any external or internal entity? This same argument should be stated regarding both non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Their permanence merely indicates an unchanging state due to their being nothing at all; it is not a positive prescription. Therefore, space and the others do not possess permanence.

Here [the opponent] says: "Space is indeed eternal because it is all-pervasive (*vibhu*); that which is impermanent is not all-pervasive, just like a jar. To this it is replied: Although by demonstrating the non-existence of that which is unarisen, the impossibility of any substratum existing within it has also been established by implication, nevertheless—desiring to expose the irrationality of that [opponent's] view by way of refuting the specific nature of categories as established in their own system, and wishing to refute the eternity of space by denying its all-pervasiveness—he says:
In a locus, not every part is called a "part";
therefore, it is very clear that there must also be another part within the locus.

Those parts which belong to space are its "locations" (*pradeśa*); by means of those locations, space is that which possesses locations (*pradeśin*). Within that [space], the location that is conjoined with a jar does not exist in the location conjoined with other objects. For if it were to exist there, then—

Therefore, even a pot that occupies a non-distinct location would have to be omnipresent; yet this is not the case, so [the opponent's position] is untenable. Furthermore, if a "location" (pradeśa) were also to exist everywhere, then because it too would be all-pervasive, it could no longer be designated as a "location," just like the thing occupying the location (pradeśin). And due to the absence of a location, there would also be an absence of the thing occupying the location. Now, if—wishing to avoid this fault—it is maintained that the thing called a "location" does not exist in its entirety within the thing occupying the location, then necessarily...

It is clearly evident that another part (*pradeśa*) must also be admitted to exist within the possessor of parts (*pradeśin*). Consequently, for space (*ākāśa*), which possesses parts that are not all-pervading, its omnipresence (*vibhutva*) would be lost—just as it is with a jar or similar objects. Furthermore, since no so-called "possessor of parts" is perceived apart from the mere collection of parts that are mutually non-distinct, how can there be permanence for something whose very existence is unestablished? Thus, space is not eternal.

Furthermore, if its state of having spatial parts is not admitted because it is partless, then in that case, there could be no conjunction even with jars and the like. For that conjunction of theirs would have to occur either by way of its entire self or by way of a single part.

It cannot be [the case that space is all-pervading] in its entirety, because it would follow that even jars and other such objects are each individually omnipresent. Therefore, one must necessarily admit that jars and the like occupy only specific locations. For one who accepts this, the aforementioned fault certainly does not apply. And because of the consequence of the aforementioned fault, space is not eternal.

The proponent of time (*kālavādin*), however, maintains the following: having observed that the activity and withdrawal of the world are brought about by time, the existence of time is inferred. For instance, even when the conditions known as seed, earth, water, fire, air, and space are present, the emergence of a sprout and so forth is not observed at all times; rather, it is observed only at certain times. Furthermore, it ceases when there is the proximity of time, which opposes its persistence in that state. Thus it is.
In whatever state both engagement and withdrawal are perceived.

That time which is thus inferred does exist; and although it exists, its eternity [is asserted] because no cause for its production is perceived. But if this were the case, since time is eternal, it would follow that sprouts and other effects dependent upon it would arise at all times. If, on the other hand, it is imagined that even though it exists, its activity toward the performance of effects is sometimes suspended, even so, that very suspension will result in its non-existence. Or, if it is argued that although it exists, there is no effect at all times because a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) within its nature—capable of initiating the production of effects—is not present, as is the case with seeds and the like.

Otherwise, there would be no cessation of saṃsāra, just as there is none for a second self. Furthermore, if one accepts a distinction [between the selves], it would be subject to change due to the existence of modification; and what is impermanent would become a cause. Consequently, it would be exactly like the continuum of suffering. This being the case, there would be a renunciation of one's own doctrine. Therefore, it is not logical to accept this self. For even if one does accept it, since it is incapable of being demonstrated to another and because of the aforementioned faults, what is the use of accepting it? Thus, let the doctrine of the self be abandoned.

If this is so, then even in the state of liberation, the liberated self would be non-existent, and Nirvana—designated as the ultimate reality (paramārtha)—would be described as the total exhaustion of the formative forces (saṃskāras) through their non-rearising; therefore, enough with such an ultimate reality that is desired [only] by one who seeks [their own] self-destruction. Thus it is said: "for one who desires the self."
This mundane [reality] alone is preferable, for the ultimate truth is not found in every respect;
something exists within the mundane, but nothing exists within the ultimate.

For one who desires their own welfare does not perform the gouging out of their eyes for fear of an affliction of vision; rather, they effect only the removal of that affliction. Likewise, for one distressed by the suffering of saṃsāra, the abandonment of suffering alone is superior, but not the total non-existence of everything. For if there were the non-existence of everything, then by the complete eradication of even happiness, nothing would have been done for this self.
Therefore, this [state] is better as something merely worldly.

For in the worldly [convention], you accept some things—namely, that which is dependently originated and designated based on [causes]; yet you do not accept other things, such as the unreal imputations by the non-Buddhists and the intrinsic nature (*sasvābhāvya*) of entities. Alternatively, in your worldly [view], there exists past karma that has not yet yielded its fruit, its future fruit, and present conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*); everything else beyond that does not exist. It would be better, therefore, to accept this much of the worldly [convention].

Therein, it is not the case that everything is non-existent; however, the ultimate reality (paramārtha) is not superior in every respect, because even the self (*ātman*) does not exist in every respect.
In the Bodhisattvayogācāra-catuḥśataka, the ninth chapter, titled "The Refutation of the Meaning of Permanence."
CHAPTER X.
Here it is said: If there were such a thing as a self by way of its own intrinsic nature, then because one would perceive its total annihilation at the time of nirvāṇa.
"I do not exist, I shall not exist; mine does not exist, mine shall not exist"—
for one who suspects [this], it would be better indeed to have the worldly [view].
The Veda is not the ultimate truth in every respect;
that which exists in the worldly realm does not exist in the ultimate truth.

Thus, no such thing as a self exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). For if it did exist, it would necessarily be either female, male, or neuter, since there is no other possible conceptualization apart from these. Indeed, the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) describe the self as being of two kinds: namely, the inner self (*antarātman*) and the outer self (*bahirātman*). Of these, the inner self—

That which is situated within the house of the body is the internal operative person (*antarvyāpārapuruṣa*), the director of the aggregate of the body and senses here and there; it is bound by the egoism of the world, the enjoyer of the fruits of actions such as the wholesome, and is divided into many distinct conceptual varieties according to each individual system. The external self (*bahirātman*), however, consists of the collection of the body and senses and acts as a benefactor to the internal self.

In that regard, if this internal self were to be conceived as female, then because it does not abandon its own essential nature, [there would be no change] even through transformation in another birth.

Even in the absence of other indicative marks, femininity would have to be eternal; however, this is not observed, because we perceive changes [in gender] and because femininity and the rest lack the status of being qualities of the self (*ātman*). The same should be stated regarding masculinity and neuter-ness.
Thus, when the inner self (*antarātman*) is neither female, nor male, nor neuter—
At that time, due solely to ignorance, you have the notion, "I am a person."

The notion "I am a man" is an illustration; likewise, "I am a woman" or "I am a neuter"—all such [notions] arise from ignorance (*ajñāna*). Since the reality of an object, when subjected to investigation, is not established as being so [as it appears], it is logical that there is no cause for such conceptual construction other than ignorance. The intended meaning is that this is like the superimposition of a snake upon a rope when the true nature of the rope is not recognized. Thus, it is established that the conceptualization of femininity and so forth regarding the inner self does not conform to reality.

Now, if you think that these marks—femininity, masculinity, and neuter-ness—belong to the external self, and are therefore attributed to the internal self through connection with it; this might indeed be so if these were applicable even to the external self. How so? In this regard, first of all, of space...

Because it is impossible for [the body] to consist of more than the great elements (*mahābhūta*), there are only four great elements. Even for one who asserts five great elements, since it is impossible for space (*ākāśa*) to be a producer of the body, only the four great elements function as its causes. Furthermore, the states of female, male, and neuter do not exist within those [elements] by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*). If they did exist, then—conforming to that intrinsic nature—all bodies would necessarily possess a fixed gender. Moreover, the gender would have to be perceived even from the *kalala* stage [of embryonic development], yet this is not the case; therefore [gender is not inherent in the elements].
When in all beings there is no female, male, or neuter,
then how can those very beings, once encountered, become female, male, or neuter?

What indeed is the reason here that, having encountered the great elements which are by their very nature devoid of gender, women, men, and neuter beings would come into existence within bodies? Thus, since even for the external self there is no connection with the states of being female, male, or neuter, this notion of yours—"I am a man," "I am a woman," or "I am a neuter"—arises solely from ignorance.

Furthermore, as for those who otherwise imagine femininity and so forth due to the absence of a cause—such as the presence of hair on the breasts and other parts of the *khaṭvā* tree and the *vṛkṣa* tree—their mere conceptualization is not prevented. If you argue that this same consequence applies to you as well, it is not so; for according to me, all things are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) because they are dependently originated, and there is no [femininity] in that which lacks intrinsic nature.

Just as a change of state according to conditions is not tenable for that which has an intrinsic nature—just as it is not tenable for the forms of a variegated man or an illusory woman—the aforementioned fault does not apply. However, for one who maintains the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvavādin*), because a change of state is impossible for an intrinsic nature, it would follow that the restriction of gender must correspond to the intrinsic nature itself. Thus, since conceptual constructions such as "I am a man" arise solely from delusion (*moha*), it is illogical for a self possessing gender to exist by way of its own nature. Furthermore, the self does not exist by way of its own nature;
for if the self did exist by way of its own nature, then just as it would be the objective support (*ālambana*) for one instance of the conceit "I," so too [would it be for all].

Furthermore, the object of the notion of "I" (ahaṅkāra) would have to be common to all; for in the world, heat is the intrinsic nature of fire, and no one possesses non-heat as its nature. Likewise, if the self existed by way of its own essence, it would be the self of everyone and the object of the notion of "I" for everyone. But this is not the case. For instance:
That which is your self is not my self; therefore, by that very fact, it is not [my] self through restriction.

For that which is your self—the object of your ego-conception (*ahaṅkāra*) and the object of your attachment to self (*ātmasneha*)—is precisely my non-self, because it is not the object of our ego-conception and not the object of our attachment to self. Since this is so, by that very rule, it is not [the self]. And that which, by rule, is not the self does not exist by its own nature; thus, the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of a self upon what is unreal is abandoned. If the self does not exist, where then do these two—the ego-conception and attachment to self—reside? To this he says:
Indeed, it is only regarding impermanent entities that what is called conceptual construction arises.

According to the reasoning already described, since a self that is distinct from the aggregates and established in its own nature is non-existent in every respect, is it not rather the case that the notion of a "self" is a mere conceptual construction applied to the impermanent entities known as form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?

The superimposition of unreal objects is performed [by claiming] "self," "sentient being," "living soul," or "creature. For just as fire exists in dependence upon fuel, so too is the self designated in dependence upon the aggregates (*skandhas*). When that [self] is analyzed in five ways—in terms of its identity with or difference from the aggregates—it does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); thus, it is conceptually constructed as a dependent designation (*upādāya-prajñapti*). Therefore, it is established that the conceptualization of a self occurs with respect to these impermanent conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāras*).

Regarding this, [an opponent] says: The self certainly exists by way of intrinsic nature, because it is the cause of engagement and cessation. For if the self did not exist, who would [perform] the good or the evil?

Or, having performed an action, one would experience its fruit. For, having performed a wholesome or unwholesome action, one encounters within the three realms—divided by distinctions such as birth, destiny, and womb—an uninterrupted succession of births corresponding to that action, with infinite variations, which serves as the basis for experiencing the fruits of pleasure and pain. He is indeed both the agent who performs the formation and the experiencer who undergoes it; he is struck, afflicted, touched, bound, and liberated. Therefore, the self exists by way of its own intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, does this self conform to the transformations of different bodies throughout the transitions of successive births, or not? If it does not conform, then what is the use of this useless conceptualization of a self? But if it does conform, then necessarily, like the body, the person undergoes transformation in birth after birth.
And consequently,
its being distinct from your body and its permanence are not tenable.

This [self] is not other than the body because it conforms to the modifications of the body, just like a part of the body; nor is it eternal because it is non-different from the body, just like the body's own nature. Thus, the superimposition of a self is untenable. For he (the proponent of the self) has postulated an eternal self for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma, since there is no persistence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which perish at every moment.

However, for him, the gathering of fuel would indeed be purposeless; this case is just like that. Consequently, the activity of this entire collection of transformations, beginning with Mahat, is entirely fruitless, and thus the labor expended in formulating its systematic analysis (*prakriyā*) in this treatise appears to be utterly useless.

Now, it might be argued that the *puruṣa* is of the nature of the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*), and that because consciousness is manifested through the operation of instruments such as the eyes, the *puruṣa* is the enjoyer through the manifestation of the activity of consciousness. He perceives the object by means of the accomplishment of the act of enjoying the object; for that enjoyment of the object by him consists of the activity whose essence is the function of consciousness. And that [activity] does not exist without the instruments, such as the eyes.

"How can this village of modifications be considered vain, given that it exists as a village? It is said in reply: If consciousness were of the nature of the activity of consciousness, then it would have to exist without transgressing the properties of action. And what is the property of actions? It is to have a substance as their locus and to possess mobility. For instance:
Just as there is no action [without a substratum], so too there is no substance called "the mobile" that persists until destruction.

For action consists of the operation of a substance, and it is mobile from its commencement until its destruction. Thus, trees and the like remain motionless, existing without having initiated action in the absence of the impact of wind and so forth.
However, this action of trembling, arising from the encounter with conditions such as wind, does not cease while they are moving until its destruction. Since this is the case:
"Therefore, it is not logical to say that the person exists but consciousness does not."

Just as trees and the like are perceived in their substantial form (*dravyarūpa*) as trees and so forth prior to the commencement of the activity of movement, the person (*puruṣa*) is not like this; for, because he consists solely of the nature of consciousness (*caitanya*), he is not distinct from it. Furthermore, since he lacks the nature of a substance, it cannot be postulated that he exists as a self devoid of consciousness.

Consequently, it is not tenable to say that the *puruṣa* exists while consciousness (*caitanya*) does not. Furthermore, the supposition that the existence of the *puruṣa* is inferred from the presence of the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*) is also incorrect, because a power cannot exist without a substratum. Just as a person cannot possibly exist apart from the functioning of consciousness, so too, even in the state of potentiality (*śakty-avasthā*), there is no *puruṣa* distinct from the mere power of consciousness. Therefore, there is no power without a support; and due to the absence of power, there can be no manifestation of power.

The claim that the eyes and other sense organs possess utility because they are useful for [producing] mental states is indeed untenable; this is certain. For it has been said: "If eternal consciousness were to arise, it would be a false instrument."
Moreover, if this person were of the nature of the power of consciousness prior to the manifestation of consciousness, then...
The element of volition is seen in one place, while the volition itself is in another.

In the hypothesis that consciousness possesses two forms, you must perceive elsewhere, as something distinct, the thinking, the element of consciousness (*cetanā-dhātu*), the seed of consciousness, and the power of consciousness; and yet, the thinking proceeding from the power of consciousness proceeds as something distinct from it, though occupying the same location as the element of consciousness. He provides an illustration:
Just as fluidity belongs to iron.

Just as iron, when undergoing liquefaction, comes to occupy a location non-different from the location of the iron itself, so it is here. For, since the appearance and disappearance of the seed and the sprout are observed, they do not occupy the same location; nor do the appearance and disappearance of the *puruṣa* [occur in such a way], and thus there is no identity of location for them. It is for this very reason that the Teacher has cited the example of the liquefaction of iron. Furthermore, the *puruṣa* does not exist separately from the nature of the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*), because the manifest is non-different from that [power]. Therefore, this [consciousness], having assumed the form of a power, undergoes the state of manifestation.
Therefore, the person undergoes a transformation, just as iron undergoes the state of liquefaction.
Furthermore, because it is subject to transformation, it is established that this self lacks permanence, just like iron.
Others, however, say: "Indeed, for us, the person is not of the nature of consciousness; what then?"
And consciousness resides in the mind alone; the Great Person is like space.

For the self (*ātman*) of all living beings is omnipresent in every body like space; however, its consciousness, being conjoined with the mind alone, is not all-pervading. And the mind is conjoined with the self only in a space as small as an atom. By being conjoined with that mind, the person (*puruṣa*) produces consciousness in a location non-different from it. Therefore, the aforementioned faults do not apply to our position. To this it is replied: since you indeed admit that for the person, who is as vast as space, consciousness resides in the mind alone—surely [this is so] according to you.
Consequently, its lack of consciousness appears as if it were its very nature.

This being the case, it follows that the *puruṣa* is indeed insentient. For it is not reasonable to say that the *puruṣa* becomes sentient through a connection with consciousness occupying a space as small as a single atom (*paramāṇu*). Indeed, it is impossible to conceive that the water of the Ganges River becomes salty merely by contact with a single atom of salt; this [proposed theory] is just like that. Furthermore, since the self (*ātman*) is a substance (*dravya*) and consciousness (*caitanya*) is of the nature of a quality (*guṇa*), the person (*pumān*) remains essentially insentient due to the mutual difference between those two.

Furthermore, it is not logical to postulate selfhood for this [body], which is insentient like a jar; thus, the self is not tenable. Moreover, if this self were omnipresent in every sentient being, then—
But another says: "If I am all-pervading, why does he not know me?"

If, according to your conception, I were all-pervading and omnipresent like space, then since my self would exist within other beings as well, why does the "I-conceit" (*ahaṃkāra*) not arise in them toward that [self] just as it does in me? For its omnipresence would be logical only if the "I-conceit" regarding my own self were to arise in another person toward my self as well. Furthermore, it is not logical for this self of mine to be obstructed by the self of another within another's body; for there is no absence of our selves in the location of another's self, since all selves are omnipresent.
Because pervasiveness is admitted; and since they occupy the same location, it is impossible for one to act as an obstruction to the other. Demonstrating this, he says:
Therefore, it is not logically possible for that very thing to be its own obscuration.
Thus [it is said].

Because they occupy the same location, there can be no obscuration by one's own self, just as there is none for the nature of the self itself; thus, it would follow that even the Supreme Self (parātman) would be an object of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). But since this is not the case, the self is not omnipresent. Having thus demonstrated that the existence of the self is untenable according to both views, he speaks next to demonstrate the untenability of the qualities (guṇas) as well, on the grounds that they cannot possibly be the creators of the entire world: [The text continues with the verse: "Since the qualities are devoid of consciousness, they are incapable of action; therefore, the world is not produced by the qualities. (SK 17ab) He explains: "If the qualities were to act, they would act either through their own power or through the power of another. They cannot act by their own power, because they are insentient (acetana), like a clod of earth or a stone. Nor can they act through the power of another, because they lack a conscious agent. Therefore, the world is not produced by the qualities. He asks: "But surely the qualities act when impelled by the Puruṣa? He replies: "No, because the Puruṣa is indifferent (udāsīna). He asks: "How so? He replies: "Because the Puruṣa is pure (śuddha) and inactive (niṣkriya). Since the Puruṣa is pure, it does not instigate the qualities toward activity, nor does it obstruct them from activity. Furthermore, since the Puruṣa is inactive, it does not instigate the qualities toward activity, nor does it obstruct them from activity. Therefore, the qualities do not act through the power of the Puruṣa. Thus, the world is not produced by the qualities. He asks: "But surely the qualities act when impelled by Time (kāla)? He replies: "No, because Time is merely a designation for the sequence of changes in the qualities themselves. He asks: "How so? He replies: "Just as one says, 'Time has passed' or 'Time remains,' in reality it is the qualities themselves that undergo change and are designated by the term 'Time. Therefore, the world is not produced by Time. He asks: "But surely the qualities act when impelled by Necessity (niyati)? He replies: "No, because Necessity is merely a designation for the fixed order of the qualities themselves. He asks: "How so? He replies: "Just as one says, 'This is the necessity of the seed' or 'This is the necessity of the sprout,' in reality it is the qualities themselves that possess a fixed order and are designated by the term 'Necessity. Therefore, the world is not produced by Necessity. He asks: "But surely the qualities act when impelled by Chance (yadṛcchā)? He replies: "No, because Chance is merely a designation for the absence of a cause. He asks: "How so? He replies: "Just as one says, 'This happened by chance' or 'That happened by chance,' in reality it is the absence of a cause that is designated by the term 'Chance. Therefore, the world is not produced by Chance. Consequently, the world is not produced by the qualities. He asks: "But surely the qualities act when impelled by the Lord (īśvara)? He replies: "No, because the Lord is unproven. He asks: "How so? He replies: "Whether the Lord is eternal or non-eternal, his existence is not established. If he were eternal, he would be subject to the same defects as the Puruṣa, and thus could not be the creator. If he were non-eternal, he would be subject to the same defects as the qualities, and thus could not be the creator. Therefore, the Lord is unproven. Consequently, the world is not produced by the Lord. He asks: "But surely the qualities act when impelled by Nature (prakṛti)? He replies: "No, because Nature is insentient. He asks: "How so? He replies: "Just as an insentient clod of earth or stone does not act without being impelled by someone, so too Nature, being insentient, cannot act without being impelled by someone. Therefore, the world is not produced by Nature. Thus, since the qualities are devoid of consciousness, they are incapable of action; therefore, the world is not produced by the qualities. He replies: "If the conjunction were eternal, the world would never cease. If it were non-eternal, it would require a cause, and thus the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā) would follow. Therefore, the conjunction is unproven. Consequently, the world is not produced by the conjunction of the Puruṣa and Nature. Thus, since the qualities are devoid of consciousness, they are incapable of action; therefore, the world is not produced by the qualities. He replies: "The same argument applies as before regarding the conjunction of the Puruṣa and Nature. Therefore, the world is not produced by the conjunction of the Puruṣa, Nature, and Time. Thus, since the qualities are devoid of consciousness, they are incapable of action; therefore, the world is not produced by the qualities. There is no difference whatsoever between those who claim that qualities possess agency and are entirely devoid of consciousness, and those who are truly insane.

Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities (*guṇa*). Their state of equilibrium is *pradhāna*; their state of evolution is *prakṛti*. Now, although this *prakṛti*, consisting of the three qualities, is insentient, it enters into a non-differentiation with the *puruṣa* due to the latter’s longing for the enjoyment of objects already known, and [thereby]... all [effects].

*Lam* gives birth to the group of transformations (*vikāragrāma*). And therein, this is the sequence: namely, from *prakṛti* comes the Great One (*mahat*); "the Great One" is a synonym for the intellect (*buddhi*). From the Great One comes the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and it is of three kinds: *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*. Among these, from the *sāttvika* ego-sense arise the five sense organs of cognition—ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—and the five organs of action, known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
And the mind, being of both natures, functions as the eleventh [sense] from the rājasa ego.

The five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; from these subtle elements arise the gross elements known as ether, air, fire, water, and earth. However, the *ahaṅkāra* characterized by *tamas* is the instigator of both types of *ahaṅkāra*. Thus, since the entire aggregate of evolutes consists of the nature of both the primary matter (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikāra*), the three *guṇas* are the instigators. This is the intention of those proponents for whom the *guṇas* possess agency yet lack consciousness. To those who are experts in the reality of things, there is no difference whatsoever between such people and madmen.

Thus they perceive. For one who is called "insane" is indeed a continuum of consciousness that is inverted; by means of that inverted consciousness, he does not understand things as they truly are, he grasps them erroneously, and he prattles on about non-existent objects. In the same way, this Sāṃkhya, who establishes through his treatise that the insentient *guṇas* possess agency, does not understand things as they truly are, he grasps them erroneously, and he prattles on about non-existent objects. Thus, he is considered exactly equal to those who are insane.

Moreover, this person is the non-agent and the enjoyer of the aggregate of modifications, whereas the *guṇas* are the agents but not the enjoyers. Thus, by asserting that agency belongs to the *guṇas* while enjoyership belongs to the Self—thereby presenting something entirely devoid of logical justification—he reveals his own utter irrationality; demonstrating this, he says:
The qualities (guṇas) indeed know how to construct houses and so forth in every respect, yet they do not know how to enjoy them; what could be more improper than this?

The intention is that because this doctrine contradicts reason and is not accepted by the world, there is nothing more irrational than it; thus, first of all, the agency of the qualities (guṇas) is untenable. Furthermore, for one who holds the view that the self alone is the agent of merit and demerit and the enjoyer of their fruit, the eternality of that self is also untenable, because:
One who performs actions does not exist eternally.

One who acts here is an agent (*kartṛ*). His agency is based upon action; for it is not logical that anyone who performs no action at all could be an agent without a cause. And when there is the possession of action, it necessarily precedes the action [in time]. To explain: through the displacement of its future state, it attains the state of the present by means of causes and conditions. However, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not undergo such a displacement from its own nature; thus, the permanence of the unconditioned is not like that [of conditioned phenomena]. Even if it were conceived in this way:
If the future were impermanent due to its destruction even without having been born, [then it would be so].
If that is so, then:
There is no destruction of the past; why then is it not considered eternal?

If the future is eternal because its own nature (svarūpa) exists even when it has not yet manifested, then let it be postulated that it is eternal since there is no loss of its own nature. Or rather, for what entity could impermanence possibly be postulated? And when it cannot be so postulated, then, due to the impossibility of impermanence for all entities, only eternity remains possible. In that regard, first:
This present [moment] is impermanent, and the past is not born.

First of all, this present entity does not possess impermanence; for it is designated as "present" because, being present, it has not fallen away from its own nature (*svabhāva*). That which possesses impermanence cannot be present at all, because of its connection with non-existence (*abhāva*), and because existence and non-existence cannot occur simultaneously. Thus, impermanence is not possible for that which is present. As for that which is past...

Furthermore, impermanence is not possible [in this case]. For that which has perished is called "past," and it is not logical for that which has already perished to perish yet again, because it would be purposeless, because there would be no substratum, and because it would entail the fallacy of infinite regress. Thus, first of all, this present and past [entity] does not arise as impermanent; nor is a third possibility for its impermanence tenable apart from the present and the past—so he says.
Apart from those two, no third state of existence exists for him.

When the impermanence of that which has arisen—which is the basis for impermanence—is impossible, then it would follow that for the future, which is empty of arising like space and so forth, that [impermanence] would exist; this is utterly incoherent. Furthermore, the conceptualization of the three time periods for space and so forth, which are devoid of impermanence, is not logical. Likewise, for one who maintains that entities possess intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*), the three time periods are not tenable.

Here it is said: The future entity certainly exists, because its birth is observed when the conditions are present; for the birth of that which is non-existent—such as the son of a barren woman—is not possible either before or after [the conditions]. Therefore, since its birth is observed, the future entity certainly exists. Even if this is postulated in such a way:
If an entity that arises later already exists beforehand,
