then the position of those proponents of necessity (niyativādins) does not arise falsely.

If it is imagined that an entity which exists prior to its arising is produced later by causes and conditions because it already exists in its own nature before arising, then the position of those who advocate determinism—describing the world as having a fixed nature, being causeless, devoid of human effort, and contrary to logical proof—would not be false. And yet, it is not so.

Their doctrine is false because their position contradicts both what is seen and what is not seen; since it disregards human effort (*puruṣakāra*), there would be no dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) for the world. And in the absence of that [dependent origination], the entire world would be ungraspable, like the horn of a donkey; thus, the doctrine of necessity (*niyativāda*) is illogical.

Furthermore, if the logic of this proponent of the existence of the future were valid, then the doctrine of the proponents of necessity would also be logical; therefore, the doctrine of the existence of future objects is illogical. It is also illogical for the following reason:
It is not logical that that for which origination is produced already exists;
if there were birth of what already exists, then even that which has already been born would undergo birth again.

It is not tenable that an object whose production—that is, its arising—is brought about by causes and conditions exists even prior to its birth. For if it were already existent, then there would be a birth again of that which is already present. Furthermore, a second birth of what is already existent is not logical, because it would be purposeless. Moreover, it would lead to an undesirable consequence:

an infinite regress (*aniṣṭhā-prasaṅga*), whereby a single object, being born again and again throughout *saṃsāra* without its arising ever reaching completion, would never allow for the occurrence of other distinct entities, resulting in a contradiction between cause and effect.
It might be argued: "Since this continuity of the stream of entities existing as causes and effects does indeed exist, the doctrine of the real existence of future entities is not tenable."

Here it is said: If the future did not exist, then that knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) of yogins which has the future object as its focal point would not be in accordance with reality. Yet this knowledge of yogins is indeed in accordance with reality, because it correctly prophesies future objects and because those objects exist exactly as they are. For this [knowledge] is not possible regarding things such as the son of a barren woman who do not exist. Therefore, the future certainly exists. It is replied: By way of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the future entity is seen; by what means is non-existence not seen?

It has been established that in the state prior to its arising, a future entity does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). If a non-existent thing were perceived by yogins, then even the son of a barren woman and the like would be perceived. Since both are equally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-āsattva*), it is illogical that one is seen while the other is not.

Furthermore, do yogins not perceive the future? They do not perceive it in the manner that you imagine. Rather, the future object must exist in its actual state as it will be when it reaches the present condition. This is due to the specific power of their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) projected by the force of their vows (*praṇidhi-bala*).

However, knowledge arising from that [past object] arises by conceptualizing the form of the object in such a way; it does not arise as a cognition conforming to the form of a proximate thing, like a present consciousness having blue as its objective support, because that would entail that the object of that knowledge is itself present.

For one who maintains that categories of existence are real entities (*vastusat-padārthavādin*), as long as that entity exists, it exists precisely as its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). When there is no apprehension of the intrinsic nature of an entity, then, because that entity is in every respect non-existent, it becomes like the horn of a donkey; thus, since he does not transcend dualistic discourse, everything he intends to establish becomes impossible to accomplish.

For those who maintain that all things lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), however, since the essential nature of any entity is impossible in every respect, the conceptualization of existence is cast far away. For that which is to arise cannot be non-existent; if it were non-existent, its arising would be impossible, like that of a donkey's horn. On the other hand, if it were existent, its arising would be impossible, just as it is for a present thing. Yet, since its arising does indeed occur, this doctrine of non-duality (*advayavāda*) is established.
Precisely because it is not non-existent, the perception of the future is not contradictory; and precisely because it is not existent, [the perception of the past is not contradictory].

In this way, even the designation of the future is established. Furthermore, since this is worldly convention and not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), a strictly logical proof is not introduced here.

As for the knowledge of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, regarding the future: it arises from the power of hearing words that correctly convey [the meaning] as projected by the empowerment of their previous vows; it arises through the emergence of consciousness permeated by such forms, within a stream of consciousness transformed by the influence of specific karmas conducive to hearing such Dharma; and having understood that object through the empowerment of the Tathāgatas, [they know it].

People perceive things according to their true nature, and at a later time, they understand that very object—once it has become present—in exactly that same way; thus is the knowledge of the Buddhas regarding the future established. It is not, however, that those [beings] see or describe anything while the dharmas remain fixed in their prior intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); enough of this digression.
Thus, for one who asserts the real existence of future entities, the perception of the future is impossible.

Furthermore, for one who holds that a future object exists by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*), that object would not be distant; yet, for such a person, its distance is indeed admitted. Since it is accepted [in the scriptures] that "Which phenomena are distant?
Those of the past and future. Which phenomena are near? Those of the present," the future is distant for him. Demonstrating that this distance of his is illogical, he says:
For whom the future exists, for him the distant does not exist.
The intention is that [the present exists] because of its actual presence.

Furthermore, whatever dharma consists of generosity, ethical conduct, and so forth, which arises from future conditions such as association with spiritual friends, hearing the Dharma, and the maturation of the faculties—that too certainly exists, because one asserts the real existence of future objects. At that time:
If dharma exists even when unperformed, then the rule [of moral causality] becomes useless.

Since that dharma for the sake of which his restraint of body, speech, and mind exists is already present in him even though unmanifested, his exertion in disciplined observance (*niyama*) for its acquisition is futile; for that dharma is possible even without it. Now, if it is argued that some excellence (*viśe�șa*) of that dharma is produced by that observance, then since that very excellence did not exist previously but is created later, his doctrine of the [dharma's] pre-existent nature (*sadbhāva*) is contradicted. Demonstrating this, he says:
Now, even if it were performed to a very small degree, the accomplishment of the goal would not be possible.

Moreover, for one who accepts that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, since impermanence is non-deviant throughout the three time periods, that which is their impermanence must necessarily be non-existent in both the prior and subsequent portions [of the present]. For in this way, its impermanence is established. If, however, it were to exist even in the two states prior to and after its arising, then it would follow that it is permanent. Now, if impermanence is admitted by him, then for him...
If [the cause] is impermanent, how indeed could there be an effect that exists [in it] beforehand?
Chapter XII. 1.

It is certain that liberation is attained through practice; and since all heretics likewise maintain that nirvāṇa is achieved by the renunciation of everything, I have not introduced anything here that is unprecedented which could serve as a cause for aversion.

For those very entities whose cessation through non-occurrence in *nirvāṇa* was intended, it is precisely for them that I have, by means of this treatise devoted to establishing their lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), performed the clearing of the thorns of false views from the path leading to the city of *nirvāṇa*. Why then do you fear, having inscribed this unreal thing in your heart?
Let your mind find satisfaction; let this Dharma be made your own; let the discourse on the warding off of defiled things be established in your consciousness.

Now, if even all the heretics share this very intention—that is, that nirvāṇa is attained through the renunciation of everything—what then is the distinction between you and those outsiders? This is the distinction: for the outsiders there is merely the intention of renouncing everything, but not the teaching of the means for renouncing everything; and since the means for renouncing everything has not been taught [by them].
What can he accomplish through renunciation who does not know that renunciation is the means?

Even if one abides in the intention of total renunciation, if they are a follower of the views of non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) and are ignorant of the means of renunciation, how could they effect renunciation? For they do not know the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), which is the means of renouncing everything and has the characteristic of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnyatā) of all phenomena. Precisely for this reason:
"Therefore, the sage surely said that there is no other auspiciousness."

It is determined that the Sage spoke thus with this very intention: "In this world there is one first ascetic, here a second, and so on up to a fourth; the doctrines of others are empty of ascetics. And from this very exposition of the means for relinquishing everything, the Blessed Buddha’s status as a teacher of reality is recognized everywhere through the unimpeded operation of his knowledge.

Furthermore, because the non-Buddhists lack the capacity to explain the means for the relinquishment of everything, their cognition regarding other categories of things is established as being erroneous; therefore, [their error] is not something to be proven.

But surely, for you too, since the objects of knowledge are infinite, when supersensuous matters are taught, doubt arises because they are not perceptible—namely, whether this object is exactly as it was taught or otherwise; for there is no cause for certain knowledge regarding such a subject. To that also, it is said:
He who develops doubt regarding the non-evident things taught by the Buddha must, in this very life, cultivate conviction toward emptiness.

For not all entities are accessible through perceptual knowledge; there are also those accessible through inference. And it is possible to formulate an inference here, because of the existence of examples. In this case, however...

The nature of all phenomena is emptiness; and that cannot be rendered otherwise by anyone. This matter is subtle, for although it is eternally present, it is not perceived by ordinary people. Its suchness has been established through reasoning by way of refuting the grasping at the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. Let your certainty be established right here: is this exactly so, or is it otherwise?
If there is any cause for uncertainty regarding this, let it be pointed out, provided that it has not already been refuted.

By means of the certainty established in the section to be explained hereafter, it is impossible for him [the Buddha] to state even the slightest cause for uncertainty; thus, this example is indeed proven. Consequently, let it be understood that any other word of the Blessed One that conveys an imperceptible object is also true to reality, because it was taught by the Tathāgata through his own method (*svanaya*), just like the words that express the meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Therefore, how could there be any room for doubt regarding those things spoken by the Buddha that are beyond perception?
Furthermore, it is not possible for non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*) to do as the Tathāgata does.

Their status as proponents of erroneous meanings can be determined simply by observing their perversion; for they teach that the activity of this world is preceded by an eternal cause, and such [a teaching] is impossible to establish, contradicts what is perceived, and contradicts logical reasoning. Thus it is.
He by whom this world is wrongly perceived is indeed deluded regarding the next world.

For it is not possible to imagine that one whose capacity for vision is obstructed by the full moon would certainly see Arundhatī; in the same way, this non-Buddhist [teacher] [is unable to see] the world, which is called the realm of sentient beings and the receptacle-world.

When one does not even correctly perceive a gross object due to being utterly deluded by the fruit [of one's own views], how could it be possible to imagine that such a person would know a most subtle object—one separated by distance of place and time, along with its various classifications? Therefore, those who thirst for the pure water of the vision of reality, in order to dispel the exhaustion and fatigue from wandering the path of saṃsāra, should not attend upon this non-Buddhist teacher, whose vision is itself completely perverted and who is like the water of a mirage;
those who follow him will be deceived for a very long time.

In this saṃsāra, which has no end and no further limit, alas, those will be deceived who—having rejected the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Teacher of reality—follow a non-Buddhist out of a desire for liberation, being deluded regarding the nature of things seen and unseen.

Why, moreover, do these seekers of liberation follow that very non-Buddhist whose vision is perverted? It is because of their fear upon hearing the teaching on the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). That fear—

"I do not exist, I shall not exist; there is nothing mine, there will be nothing mine"—grasping at this, one feels terror. This is because for a very long time one has habituated oneself to the notions of "I" and "mine. Therefore, by being taken hold of by a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one abandons like a stain even that deep-seated adherence to the intrinsic nature of phenomena which has been practiced for so long.
Those who go to nirvāṇa by themselves perform what is extremely difficult to do.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, having become enlightened by himself, proceeds alone to the city of nirvāṇa; such is he who performs this difficult task.
The mind of one who is non-existent does not venture even to follow behind its leader.

Not only does the mind of those non-existent beings, who are situated like sea-monsters within the ego-grasping, lack the resolve to go toward nirvāṇa by themselves; moreover, even the mind of this non-existent being following behind the aforementioned guide lacks the enthusiasm to go toward nirvāṇa.
Why, then, does the mind of this non-existent person following behind the guide lack the resolve to go toward nirvāṇa? Because of fear regarding emptiness.
Furthermore, for whom does fear arise regarding this? Addressing the one for whom it does arise, he says:
Fear does not arise regarding the unseen; once it is seen, it entirely departs.
Therefore, fear is prescribed specifically toward one who possesses only limited knowledge.
For cowherds and others who have not mastered the technical terminology of the treatises, even if emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is taught to them hundreds of times,

because they lack any entry into it whatsoever and have never seen the meaning of emptiness, no terror arises in them. In that regard, for one who is utterly deluded— just as with the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), or like the fire of hell for one whose mental continuum is propped up by false views— it [terror] departs entirely once [the truth] is seen.

For when the dharma called emptiness is seen, that terror completely departs from those who are wise, because of the disappearance of the clinging to a self and what belongs to a self which is the cause of fear—just as the fear of a snake vanishes for one who has mistaken a rope for a snake upon seeing it is actually a rope. Ya...

However, for one who knows only a little, fear is inevitably and necessarily produced. For a well-trained rider of a rutting elephant does not fear it even when being tossed about by a female elephant; nor does a very foolish villager who is eager to ride it fear it, because he fails to see the dangers such as falling from it and instead highly prizes the act of riding itself. But the one who knows only a little fears excessively, considering himself unskilled in that mounting.
Indeed, this is how one proceeds in all undertakings.

In that case, fear necessarily arises for one who knows only a little, but not for one who has realized reality due to their self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*). Nor does it arise for one who is completely ignorant, because such a person is sustained by delusion (*moha*). However, the one who knows only a little trembles, because the reflection arises as to whether this is possible or impossible.

But for what reason do these people of limited knowledge not seek the supreme state, until their knowledge of all that is to be known reaches its completion? It is said: out of fear. What, then, is the cause of this fear? He says: lack of practice. And what is the cause of that? It is the practice of the contrary; explaining that very point, he says:
For the foolish, practice in the dharma that leads to engagement proceeds exclusively;
because they lack practice in the dharma that leads to withdrawal, they experience fear.

For the phenomenon that is conducive to the progression of *saṃsāra* is the "impelling" (*pravartaka*) phenomenon; and for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who abide on the stages included within the level of ordinary beings, their practice consists precisely of such impelling phenomena. Indeed, the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is the "reversing" (*nivartaka*) phenomenon because it is conducive to the cessation of *saṃsāra*. Self-attachment (*ātmasneha*), however, is an obstacle to the practice of that [emptiness], because the mental continuum of ordinary beings follows after it. Therefore, ordinary beings are far removed from the phenomenon that reverses that [self-attachment].
They are terrified; regarding the emptiness of intrinsic nature as if it were a precipice, they do not venture to practice it correctly.

Thus, when the reality of things is shrouded by the dense darkness of ignorance, and for some individual whose true path has been lost in the vast wilderness of the great forest of saṃsāra—where no further limit can be perceived—if there arises a devotion toward the discourse on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, then, through the attainment of favorable conditions conducive to that, as his clarity increases accordingly regarding emptiness, so too should faith be cultivated toward the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, by one who is compassionate and grateful.

Desiring to avoid the karma that causes obstacles for oneself and serves as the cause for a great downfall, one should plunge even into danger and give even what is difficult to give; having gathered [disciples] through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), this True Dharma should be taught to those who are vessels for the True Dharma.
But as for one who not only does not hold in high regard what has been thus taught, but moreover—
Whoever, being deluded by some form of ignorance, creates an obstacle to reality, for him there is no attainment of the auspicious; what then need be said of liberation?
By some delusion—such as envy, stinginess, indolence, fear, hatred toward the listener, and so forth—with regard to the instruction on reality...

Regarding a person who creates obstacles for others—those worthy vessels—for hearing the teaching of reality and so forth: for such a person, even the possibility of a happy rebirth as a god or human being does not exist, since they will certainly go to the lower realms; how much less, then, could there be any opportunity for them to hear discourse on liberation? For what harm has he not done to his own and others' mental continuums? For by him [is obstructed] that mass of light which, spreading before the faces of all hopes without exception, possesses a most vivid illumination, functions with unimpeded power throughout the three times, and is daily accumulated for the destruction of the darkness of ignorance.
Thus, an obstruction was committed against the continuity of the lamp of wisdom, which is capable of illuminating the dispositions of the entire world as it arises in its stream.
In this very way, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, seeing the extreme harm caused to both himself and others, spoke [as follows].
It is better to fall away from ethical discipline than ever to fall away from the right view.
Thus [it is said].
It is stated in the Sūtra:
"Better is one who has failed in ethical discipline than one who has failed in view.
In order to demonstrate the logical justification for these words of the Tathāgata, the Master said:
By ethical conduct one goes to heaven;
by right view one goes to the supreme state.
Thus it is said.

For the failure of ethical discipline (*śīlavipatti*), when accumulated through mild, medium, and intense degrees, proceeds with a definite limit of its maturation (*vipāka*) as the fruit of rebirth among hungry ghosts, animals, and in the hells—provided that one does not harbor malice toward Noble Ones (*ārya*) who have attained right view. However, for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet attained right view, the purity of ethical discipline (*śīlaviśuddhi*) results preeminently in the fruit of heaven. But the failure of vision (*darśanavipatti*), even if it is milder, cannot be equaled in the magnitude of its maturation by even hundreds of thousands of incalculable instances of the failure of ethical discipline, let alone surpassed.

Now, if by some means, through the convergence of conditions, this person were to achieve the perfection of right view through the arising of the Noble Path, then, having utterly dispelled the darkness of ignorance that has proceeded from beginningless saṃsāra and having placed the entire realm of sentient beings before him, he would surely attain nirvāṇa. Having thus understood the exceedingly great purpose of this vision of reality, the wise person should strive so that it may not be obstructed; nor should they harbor any fear of its obstruction.

A wise person, unable to discern the specific qualities of a recipient in all cases, should not teach this vision of selflessness to those who are unworthy vessels; for teaching it to the unworthy would lead only to harm. And for this very reason:
Egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is better for one who is unreal than the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

For one who lacks conviction in the dharmas of selflessness and is instead obsessed with the grasping at a self is called "unreal" because he follows the thicket of views by relying on false teachings. For such an unreal person, the teaching of a self is preferable, because it is conducive to the cessation of misconduct; for, through the persistence of attachment to a self, he [refrains from evil].

Desiring this for himself, he highly values the cessation of misconduct; and for one who has desisted from evil, rebirth in a happy realm becomes easily attained. The teaching of selflessness, through its realization of the rejection [of the self] and the correction of error, certainly destroys the continuum of body and mind. Thus it is.
One goes only to ruin, while the other goes only to auspiciousness.

For the ignorant person who has fallen into error regarding the vision of selflessness goes only to a state of ruin, not to the auspicious; whereas he who is not the other goes only to the auspicious, not to ruin. This word "other" (itara) denotes that which is not superior. And who is he?

The inferior one is he who either misunderstands or rejects the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). By the negation of that [inferiority], "the other" is not meant; "not the other" means the superior one. Precisely because of the teaching of emptiness, whereas the other ends in ruin, from that very teaching of emptiness the "other" arises as one who ends in *nirvāṇa*. Through the condition of seeing emptiness, by abandoning all attachments everywhere, one whose mass of afflictions and karma has been destroyed certainly attains extinction.
Furthermore, what indeed is this so-called selflessness (nairātmya), which is not to be taught when [the self] does not exist, but is to be taught when it does? Explaining that, he says:
The non-dual gateway to Śiva, which strikes fear into those of wrong views and is the domain of all Buddhas— this is what is called selflessness (nairātmya).

That which is the non-dual door to the auspicious (*śiva*) is selflessness (*nairātmya*). That which is terrifying to those with wrong views is selflessness. That which is the object (*viṣaya*) of all the Buddhas is called selflessness. In this context, "self" (*ātman*) refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities that is independent of anything else; the absence of that is selflessness. And that [selflessness] is understood as twofold through the distinction between phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*): namely, the selflessness of phenomena and the selflessness of persons.

In this context, what is called a "person" (pudgala) is that which, as the appropriator of the five aggregates known as appropriation, is designated in dependence upon the aggregates; and it [is sought] among the aggregates in five ways.

When sought, [the person] is not found. However, "dharmas" are entities designated as aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). This is because these dharmas and the person arise dependent upon their respective causes and conditions, and because they are designated in dependence [upon other factors]. Since there exists no self-dependent, independent, innate, or unconditioned nature, the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) is established for both the person and the dharmas. For that entity whose own-form is not established, how could it be established through any other essence? Thus, they are entirely devoid of an established specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, when entities exist—whether through being perceived or through being grasped—in a manner that is deceptive, they become the locus of attachment for those of deluded intellect. However, when they are correctly contemplated by means of right vision according to their true nature, they bring about the complete exhaustion of attachment to both phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*). And the exhaustion of attachment is the cause for attaining *nirvāṇa*.

Selflessness (*nairātmya*) is the peerless gateway to peace; it is the sole, solitary gateway for entering the city of *nirvāṇa*. Although there are three gateways to liberation known as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), nevertheless...

The vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*) alone is paramount. For one who has realized selflessness and whose attachment to phenomena has been utterly exhausted, there is no longing whatsoever for anything, nor is there any perception of signs; thus, this selflessness is the peerless gateway to the auspicious (*śiva*). And this very [selflessness] is terrifying to those of wrong views. "Wrong views" (*kudṛṣṭi*) refers to contemptible views. Since no entity is perceived in any way within selflessness, and because those of wrong views rely upon the conceptual construction of the intrinsic nature of entities and perceive an absolute annihilation, this selflessness is terrifying to them.

Selflessness (*nairātmya*) is the object (*viṣaya*) of all Buddhas. "Of all Buddhas" refers to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Buddhas (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbuddhas*). It is called "the object of all Buddhas" because it exists as the domain of their specific gnosis (*jñāna-viśeṣa*). Alternatively, indicating that it exists inseparably from the Dharma-body (*dharma-śarīra*) of all perfectly complete Buddhas, he says, "the object of all Buddhas. The Master has described selflessness by means of its specific characteristics; however, this selflessness should not be taught to those who exist [in the world] and possess dull intellects. Why? Because:
Even from the mere name of this Dharma,
fear arises in the wicked.
For because this dharma is exceedingly difficult to traverse and profound, fear arises even from hearing the word "selflessness. To illustrate:
Who indeed has ever been seen as strong who does not strike fear into another?

The vision of selflessness is powerful because it is capable of uprooting all false views; false views are weak because they are to be uprooted. It is a certainty that one who is weak fears one who is strong. Therefore, this Dharma should not be taught to one whose mental continuum has been made one's own by a weak, false view, on the grounds that it would cause fear.
Is this not so?

This Dharma must indeed be taught, because it crushes all false views; for thus, those who propound opposing doctrines must necessarily be refuted in accordance with the Dharma. Therefore, one who desires debate and seeks to conquer the positions of others should teach this Dharma even to unworthy recipients. To this it is replied: this is not so, because—
This Dharma was not taught by the Tathāgatas for the sake of debate;

if this Dharma had been taught for the sake of debate, it would be so. However, this was not taught for the purpose of debate, because it was taught by way of the gates of liberation. Even though this is so...
Chapter XIII: Refutation of the Sense Organs and Their Objects
If the eye were to see that form, would it see it by going to the location of the object or without going? Demonstrating that there is a fault in both cases, he says:
If the eye were to see after traveling a long distance over time, then why is it that a form is not clearly perceived both when it is extremely close and when it is far away?

If the eye, because it acts by reaching [its object], were to go to the location of the object, then it would not perceive objects such as the moon and stars merely upon being opened. For an object that possesses motion, it is illogical to have simultaneous perception of a nearby object and perception of a distant object, because the time taken for movement would differ. And yet, the eye does see.

It is incorrect to say that by the mere act of reaching [the object], even something situated in a distant place is perceived as if it were nearby. Furthermore, if the eye were to function by reaching its object, then it would see even what is extremely close, such as the collyrium or the applicator-stick located in the eye itself; yet it would also have to perceive distant things clearly. Since this is not possible, the claim is untenable.

Moreover, if the eye perceives an object after having traveled to it, does it go to the location of the object after seeing it, or without seeing it? Demonstrating that there is a fault in both cases, he says:
If the eye departs after seeing a form, no benefit whatsoever is gained; or else,
it would follow that the object of sight must necessarily be desired,
which is a futile conclusion.

If it is imagined that the eye goes to the location of the form after seeing the form, then there is no purpose for the eye’s movement by means of that going; for the purpose of the eye’s movement is to see the object, and since that object has already been seen while remaining here previously, there is no purpose whatsoever for the movement. Alternatively, if it goes without having seen [the object], then the seeing of the desired object is not necessarily achieved. For, like a blind person who goes to an unobserved place without having seen it, the seeing of what is to be seen is not necessarily achieved through such a movement.
If, out of a desire to avoid this fault...
The eye would grasp what has not yet arrived and see this entire world;
for that which has no movement, there is neither distance nor obstruction.

For one who, based on scripture, thinks that the eye, ear, and mind do not reach their objects—arguing that the eye does not reach its object because the scripture intends only to negate the notion that they function by reaching [the object]—to such a person it is said: there is no contradiction, since the scripture is merely intent upon negating the idea of functioning through contact. In some cases, affirmation is primary, where there is no contradiction; in other cases, negation is primary.

Where there is grain, there is no contradiction [with this principle]. Since a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is impossible in this case, its scope is established as referring to what has not been previously attained, by means of a mere prohibition of what was already occurring. If, however, its scope were conceived as referring to the unattained through a positive injunction, then the eye situated right here would see the entire world. For one that has no movement, how could there be "distance"? Indeed, even an object standing nearby must be seen by it without going, just like an object standing far away; thus, there would be no distinction made by distance. And when it sees without going, then [the distant] is just like what is situated right here.

One would see even what is far away. For it is logical that when there is motion, one does not see what is obstructed because the motion is impeded; however, when one sees the object without having gone [to it], then since there is no obstruction to motion, there should be vision as if it were unobstructed. Furthermore, if the eye were of the nature of vision, then because its nature is unimpeded everywhere, it would see even its own form. Thus, indeed, in the world...
The intrinsic nature of all things is first perceived within oneself;
by what means is the apprehension of the eye itself not produced by the eye alone?

Just as fragrance in *campaka*, jasmine, and other such flowers is first perceived in their own substrates, and subsequently [is perceived] even in oils and other substances through contact with them.

Just as heat is established in fire by its own nature, yet it is perceived in other things through connection with it, so too, if the eyes possessed the inherent nature of seeing, then seeing would first occur within the eyes themselves. Why, then, is the eye not apprehended by the eye itself? Since the intrinsic nature of entities exists most primordially within themselves, it would be logical for the eye to be apprehended by the eye alone. However, because the eye does not see its own self, just like a clod of earth or similar objects, even the perception of external objects by it is not possible.

But as for one who thinks that the eye alone does not possess the capacity to see form, but rather that the seeing of form occurs when there is a conjunction of the three—the eye, the form, and the visual consciousness—that too is without substance, because:
The eye has no consciousness, and consciousness has no seeing;
both are absent in the case of form—how then is form seen?

First of all, there is no consciousness in the eye; for the eye does not cognize its object, because its nature is not that of consciousness. Since the eye is composed of the primary elements (*bhautika*), being insentient (*jaḍa*), the cognition of an object is not possible for it; thus, consciousness does not exist in the eye. Nor does seeing belong to consciousness; for consciousness cognizes, but it does not see. If consciousness were to see, then it too would have the vision of form, due to the presence of consciousness.

But for form (*rūpa*), neither of these two exists: there is no consciousness because its nature is not that of cognition, nor is there seeing because of the absence of the observation of form. And since the sense-faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are thus mutually deficient in their respective functions, then even when their assemblage is present, it can be maintained that form is simply not seen. The intention is that, because the factors for seeing form are incomplete, it is like a group of blind people. When the seeing of form is thus impossible, what knower of reality (*tattvavid*) would be capable of saying "form is seen" or of actually seeing it?

And just as one who knows reality ought not to see form, so too ought one not to hear sound, because hearing sound is impossible in the same manner as seeing form. Here, if sound is heard, it must be heard either having reached the location of the ear or without having reached it. First, if it is heard having reached [the ear], does it travel while producing sound, or does it travel while being soundless? In that regard, if the first alternative holds:
If sound proceeds while speaking, by what means is the speaker produced? Or if it proceeds without speaking, how can there be a cognition of it?

And therefore, because it possesses the property of being spoken, this sound does not exist [prior to utterance], just like Devadatta. Now, if they say that it moves [to the ear], then while that sound is itself silent as it departs, who could have the conviction that "this sound is coming"? Furthermore, it is not logical to assert the existence of something that has not been perceived. Moreover, there is another point:
If the sound is perceived once it has reached [the ear], by whom is its beginning perceived?
Nor does the sound arrive alone; how then can it be perceived in isolation?

If sound is perceived only when it reaches the locus of the auditory faculty, then because the ear perceives only what is reached (*prāptagrāhitva*), there would be no perception of the beginning of a sound. Furthermore, since no other sense faculty could possibly perceive it, its beginning would not be perceived by anything at all. Consequently, because it is not perceived [as having a beginning], the intention is that it would not even be a "sound. Moreover, because the atom of sound consists of nine substances, a solitary sound does not exist. And since, according to you, only sound is perceived by the ear and not odors and so forth—[this would be impossible].
It is logical: either let there be no perception of sound, or let odor and the other [objects] also be perceived. Since this is not the case, sound does not have a reached object (*prāptaviṣaya*).
Now, as for what was said:
"If sound is perceived when it has been reached, by whom is its beginning perceived?"
If its beginning is not grasped in this way, then what is the fault? This is the fault: that its very nature as a word is destroyed. For it is thus:
As long as a sound is not heard, so long that sound has not come into being;
moreover, it is not logical that that which is not sound should possess the nature of sound at the end.

That which is not heard does not exist as sound at all because it is not being heard, just like odor and other such things. If you think that it will become sound when it is heard, this too is impossible; for it is never observed that odor and the like later acquire the nature of sound, and likewise, it is illogical for this [entity] which is not sound to later acquire the nature of sound. Having thus demonstrated the incapacity of the sense organs to apprehend their objects, he speaks next to demonstrate the mind's incapacity to apprehend its object:
What will the mind do, even after having gone somewhere, if it is dissociated from the sense faculties?

If it is conceived that the mind goes to the location of the object and discerns the object, that is incorrect. In this case, would this mind go to the location of the object accompanied by the sense-faculties, or alone? First of all, it does not go accompanied by the sense-faculties, because the sense-faculties are always present within the body itself; furthermore, if they were to go, it would follow that the body would be deprived of its sense-faculties.
Now, if it goes alone, then even so—
What will the mind do even after going [to an object] if it is dissociated from the sense faculties?

For this [mind], being deprived of the doors of the visual and other senses, lacks the capacity to see forms and so forth; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even the blind and others would possess the faculty of seeing and so on.

Even if it were somehow imagined that this [consciousness] perceives the object by traveling to the location of the object, even then, because the cognition of the object would never reach completion, there would be no cessation [of the process].
If this were so, why would this living being here not always be without a mind?

The self (ātman) would always be something inconceivable; yet it is not logical to conceive of the inconceivable as having the nature of a self, because, like a pillar or other such objects, it would be inconceivable.

Thus, when the sense faculties, their objects, and consciousnesses are examined through reasoning, since their existence as real entities is impossible, their establishment as having an intrinsic nature (svarūpa) is non-existent. For if these were established by way of their own nature, they would be perceived even more clearly in their actual state when examined through valid reasoning. Yet they are not so perceived. Therefore, it is established that they are empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnya).

If, then, these things have no so-called intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how is it that perception (*saṃjñā*), which consists in the discernment of their specific qualities, is taught as the cause for establishing the distinctions between entities? It is said in reply: Perception, which consists in the discernment of the specific qualities of entities, would exist only if those entities were present. Since the non-existence of those entities is being demonstrated, how could there be an establishment of their own-form (*svarūpa*) by means of that [perception]? Is it then the case that this discernment of objects does not exist at all? It is not non-existent; for an entity devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvabhāva*) does indeed exist. For instance:
That object which was previously seen and is grasped by the mind like a mirage,
within all the established arrangements of phenomena, is designated as the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).

In this case, visual consciousness arises depending on the eye and visible forms; as it ceases, it ceases together with its faculty and its object. When that has ceased, the very same object previously seen is subsequently grasped by the mind. How, then, is the apprehension of something not present possible? To this he says: "Water exists in the mirage. Furthermore, by the power of causes and conditions, the perception of the form of water indeed proceeds. Thus, [even though] non-existent...

Even with respect to an object that lacks an intrinsic nature (*asvarūpa*) and has been previously apprehended—such as a mirage—the conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-vijñāna*) that arises is the cause for the establishment of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-vyavasthā*). Because it is the cause for the establishment of all phenomena, it is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). This is due to its association with such specific types of perception. Furthermore, the establishment of all phenomena is to be understood as being by the power of perception, and not as being based on the intrinsic nature of the objects themselves, because an intrinsic nature is in every way untenable.

If this is so, then the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) must exist by way of its own nature (svabhāva), for if it did not exist, it would be impossible to establish the differentiation of all phenomena. To this it is replied: That perception, too, because it is associated with consciousness (vijñāna), does not exist apart from consciousness; and that consciousness, too, because it is not established apart from perception, does not exist by way of its own intrinsic form (svarūpa). This is because the mind arises in dependence upon the eye and forms like an illusion.

For that consciousness does not exist prior to its arising such that it could function as the locus for the activity of arising. Even though conditions such as the eye and so forth are present, because the intrinsic nature of consciousness is impossible, the activity of arising does not occur; thus, arising is not tenable.
Since this consciousness nevertheless arises, what can be concluded from this other than that its nature is like an illusion?

For it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, it is just as if a magician or a magician’s apprentice were to display various magical feats at a crossroads—such as a body of elephants, a body of chariots, or a body of infantry—and a man with sight were to see them, contemplate them, and examine them thoroughly. As he sees, contemplates, and examines them thoroughly, they would appear to him as non-existent, as empty, as hollow, and as devoid of essence."

For what reason? Is there any essence in this which is created by illusion? In the very same way, whatever consciousness there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; whether far or near—a monk should see it, contemplate it, and examine it thoroughly and fundamentally. As he sees it, contemplates it, and examines it thoroughly and fundamentally...

Even though this [consciousness] exists, it should appear to him as empty, as vain, as insubstantial, as a disease, as a tumor, as a thorn, as an evil, as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.
Why is that? Is there any core to be found in this aggregate of consciousness?
(Saṃyutta Nikāya XXII.95.12–13; parallel; SN III 142)

Since the intrinsic nature [of consciousness] is impossible when it is being analyzed in the manner in which it is perceived, it can be determined that consciousness is like an illusory maiden. Therefore, it is well said:
"Depending upon the eye and form, the mind arises like an illusion."
If, moreover, it were to have an intrinsic nature (svarūpa),
then that which exists by way of its own nature could not be called "illusion" (māyā).

For it is not tenable in the world to say that a woman who is real and not empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is an illusion (*māyā*). In the same way, consciousness (*vijñāna*) also would not be like an illusion because it exists by way of its own essential form; yet consciousness is taught to be like an illusion. Therefore, consciousness is without intrinsic nature. And when consciousness is without intrinsic nature, it is established that the perception (*saṃjñā*) associated with that consciousness without intrinsic nature is itself without intrinsic nature.
Here [the opponent] says: "This is marvelous! But how [is it so] regarding the sense faculties..."

"It is also possible that the grasping of an object occurs; for it is said that visual consciousness arises depending upon the eye and visible forms. It is replied: "Is this alone the wonder you have seen? Why is this not a wonder—that the emergence of a sprout from a seed is neither logical if the seed has already ceased, nor if it has not ceased, yet a sprout nevertheless arises depending upon the seed? In the same way, it is impossible for performed and accumulated karma that has ceased to remain anywhere at all."

Even from karma that has been extinguished for hundreds of thousands of eons, the fruit indeed arises directly. Furthermore, things such as jars, when analyzed in terms of their identity with or difference from their own causes, are not found to exist; nevertheless, through dependent designation (*upādāya prajñapti*), they become capable of performing functions such as containing and carrying honey, water, and so forth. Thus it is.
When nothing on earth is considered a marvel by the wise,
then what indeed is there to wonder at regarding the movement of the senses?

For an effect is observed to conform to its own cause: a cow from a cow, a horse from a horse, rice from rice, and so forth. However, this rule is not observed in the case of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their qualities such as form and sound. For instance, because they are perceivable by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), the great elements are invisible and inaudible; yet from them, visible form and audible sound are produced. This is truly a marvel! The same should be applied to the objects of the nose and other senses, as well as to the eye and other faculties.

Alternatively, this functioning of the sense organs toward their objects is not a cause for wonder. For if this diversity belonged solely to the sense organs in their apprehension of objects, then it would be a ground for amazement. But when the entire world, by the logic already stated, causes wonder to the wise like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), then this is no marvel. Indeed, something that is perceived as impossible only in a limited context gives rise to wonder, but not when it is of the same nature everywhere. For the heat of fire does not cause wonder.
Precisely because its essential nature is not fixed, it undergoes transformation in various ways according to the cognition of the wise.
Existence is like a whirling firebrand, a magical creation, a dream, an illusion, the moon reflected in water,
mist, an echo within a cave, a mirage, and a cloud.

Just as when a rapidly whirling firebrand is brandished, there arises the perception of a circle because it is based on a cognitive distortion regarding what is seen therein, yet not even a trace of the nature of a circle exists there; and just as emanations, produced through the condition of a specific meditative concentration (*samādhi*), bring about various distinct activities and give rise to the mental distortions of perception and cognition— such as the notion that they are real yogis— yet they are not real for yogis because they lack mind, mental factors, and sense faculties.

Just as the dream-body, which arises conditioned by a personal existence associated with consciousness conjoined with torpor, is based on a perversion of affection for the self— just like the waking body— and yet that [dream-body] is unreal because it does not appear in that way to one who has awakened;

and just as young women created by illusion through the mechanism of a magician arise solely to delude the minds of those ignorant of their true nature, while being empty of the reality of actual women.
Just as the moon in the water, though empty of a real moon, appears to fools as a moon due to the power of dependent origination and becomes a basis for the misconception [of a real moon];

and just as, by the very power of dependent origination, depending upon such causes as time, place, and signs, a mist arises and becomes a basis for the misconception of real smoke for those standing at a distance; [so too is the nature of things].
Just as an echo, arising dependently within mountain caves and the like, produces in the ignorant the conceit that it is a real sound;

and just as a mirage, appearing distinct from the nature of water due to the conditions of specific time and place and the rays of the sun, produces the error of water for those standing at a distance.

Just as clouds from a distance produce the illusion of the form of mountains and the like, so too for the ignorant—those who are unskilled in the nature of dependent origination as it truly is—the ocean of birth beginning with consciousness, conditioned by karma projected by the distortions of ignorance, appears to deceive foolish people. Although it is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaśūnya*) and characterized by falsity and deception, together with its external receptacle world, it manifests [as real]. Furthermore, those who have realized the nature of phenomena remain free from attachment everywhere. Thus, it is established that cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is without intrinsic nature, like a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*).
The thirteenth chapter, titled "The Refutation of the Objects of the Senses," in the *Bodhisattvayogācāra-catuḥśataka*, is completed.

CHAPTER XIV. Here it is said: If existence (*bhava*) is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) because it is dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), like a circle of fire (*alātacakra*) and so forth, then what could possibly have an intrinsic nature now? It is impossible to conceive of an intrinsic nature for any entity whatsoever, because such an entity is not perceived in any way at all. For instance:
If there were any state whose existence depended on nothing else anywhere, its existence might be established; yet such a thing does not exist.

For if, in the production of any entity whatsoever, nothing were dependent upon anything else, then—since that which is independent and autonomous would be established by itself—it would be logical to conceive of its existence as being due to its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). However, such a possibility does not exist; namely, that there could be no dependence for those things whose birth is contingent upon causes and conditions, or that any entity could possibly exist without a cause. And since this is so, [there can be no intrinsic nature] without a cause.

Because it would follow that some entity lacks its own essential nature (svarūpa) in certain respects, therefore no entity possesses intrinsic nature (svabhāva). And due to the absence of intrinsic nature, it is established that there is no proof of an intrinsic nature, just like a whirling firebrand (alātacakra). Furthermore, if these entities were non-deceptive—like a whirling firebrand and the like—and because they were non-deceptive, they were not unreal (avastuka), then when necessarily examined through reasoning, their essential natures would be perceived even more clearly, like gold and so forth. Yet, when heated by the fire of analysis, these do not [retain] their essential natures, because they are based on error (viparyāsa).
They do not find any real entity (*bhāva*), for even from the perspective of logical proof (*upapatti*), it is not tenable; this is because it is in every respect deceptive.
Therefore, in order to loosen attachment to real entities, the Master has stated the following reasoning as to how the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of jars and so forth is impossible.
Form itself is not the pot; there is no oneness, nor is there a pot that possesses form as something other.
Form does not exist in the pot, nor does the pot exist in form.

In this regard, if there were some entity called a "jar," it would have to be conceptualized either as distinct from visible form (*rūpa*) because it is perceptible by the visual faculty, or as non-distinct from it. First of all,
the jar is not identical to visible form.

It is not possible for form and the pot to be identical on the grounds that "whatever is form, that is the pot. For if form and the pot were identical, then wherever there is form, there would be a pot; thus, a pot would exist everywhere there is form. Furthermore, when a quality produced by baking arises and the [original] form is destroyed, the pot itself would have to be destroyed. Since this is not possible, the pot is not identical to the form; there is no oneness. Now, if one wishes to avoid this fault, [one might argue that] the pot is other than the form and possesses form.

It might be argued that, just as Devadatta is "possessed of cows" (*gomān*) by virtue of cows being distinct entities [from him], so too [the pot] would be [distinct from its form]. This, however, is incorrect. For there exists no pot other than form (*rūpa*).

If the pot were other than form, it would be perceived independently of form. Indeed, Devadatta, who is not separate from his cows, is not perceived apart from them; likewise, the pot would also be perceived independently of form. But it is not so perceived; therefore, there is no pot distinct from form.

And when [the form] does not exist, how could that which is non-existent be apprehended as possessing that [quality]? For one who is non-existent, such as the son of a barren woman, is not designated as "possessing cows. Likewise, it is also not tenable to say "the pot possesses form," precisely because of the impossibility of their being distinct; thus, even the conceptualization of a container and its contents between form and the pot is not established.
Form does not exist in the pot, nor does the pot exist in form.

If form and the pot were distinct entities, it would follow that "form is in the pot," as curd is in a bowl; or it would follow that "the pot is in form," as Devadatta is on a mat. Since this is impossible, the pot does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). That which lacks intrinsic nature yet is perceived is empty of intrinsic nature, like a firebrand-circle and the like.

Furthermore, just as the self is not the aggregates—because it would follow that the agent (the self) and the action (the appropriation) are one, because it would follow that [the self] like the aggregates is subject to arising and passing away, and because it would follow that there are many selves—so too a jar is not form, because it would follow that the appropriated (form) and the appropriator (the jar) are one, and because it would follow that there are many jars due to the multiplicity of the appropriated.

And just as the self is not other than the aggregates—because it would follow that it could be perceived separately [from them] and because it would be causeless—[so too the jar is not other than form].

And because it would follow that [the pot] is identical [to its form]. Likewise, a pot is not something distinct from its form, for that would entail the consequence of being perceived separately and the consequence of being causeless.

Just as the self is not designated as "possessing the aggregates" due to the absence of any conceptualization of its identity with or difference from the aggregates, in exactly the same way, a pot is not designated as "possessing form" due to the absence of any conceptualization of its identity with or difference from form.

Just as the conception of the self as being either identical to or different from the aggregates is untenable—since it is neither logical for the aggregates to be in the self nor for the self to be in the aggregates—likewise, the two conceptions that "form is in the pot" or "the pot is in form" are also not tenable.

And just as these fourfold conceptions regarding a pot in relation to form are impossible, so too the fourfold conceptions in relation to all causes of designation are impossible. Thus, the pot does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

And just as a jar does not exist by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*), so too all things (*bhāva*), when sought by way of their own-being, do not exist; thus it is established that existence (*bhava*) is like a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*) and the like. Regarding this, some say: "Even though a difference between form (*rūpa*) and a jar is not possible, nevertheless there is a difference between the entity (*bhāva*) and the jar. For the jar is indeed other than [the entity], and its existence (*sattā*) is of another kind. For 'existence' is the great universal (*mahāsāmānya*), while the jar is a particular (*viśeṣa*); a substance (*dravya*) is designated as 'existent' because of its connection with existence. To them, it is replied:
If, having observed the distinctness between the two, you claim that the pot is other than existence,
why will it not likewise follow that existence is also other than the pot?

Because substances such as a jar possess the characteristic of persistence (*anupravṛtti*), existence (*bhāva*) is the universal; and because the jar possesses the characteristic of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it is the particular. If, having observed the difference between those two—existence and the jar—one concludes that the jar is distinct from existence, then for the same reason of difference, why should existence not also be distinct from the jar?

Consequently, another distinctness (*anyatva*) characterized by non-occurrence—which serves as the cause for the application of a different cognition and term—need not be postulated. Since the application of a different cognition and term is established through dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) alone, if another distinctness is nevertheless postulated, then there would be no distinctness between an entity (*bhāva*) and a jar that depends upon their dissimilarity. And thus, as for what was said—that having observed the dissimilarity between two things, the jar is other than the entity—[that is untenable].
This is not so.

For just as an entity (*bhāva*) is distinct from a jar because it has the characteristic of persistence (*anupravṛtti*), so too "otherness" (*anyatva*) would have to be distinct from the jar because it also has the characteristic of persistence. Yet, there is no further "otherness" of that otherness which could serve as the cause for the application of a distinct cognition or term. If such were the case, there would be the fault of an infinite regress (*aparyavasāna*) of othernesses.

Now, if the cognition of "otherness" occurs even without actual otherness, then let it be postulated in the same way elsewhere as well; enough, then, with this useless imagined otherness. Furthermore, since otherness does not exist, it is established that nothing can be other than anything else.
Moreover, this must be considered: of what kind of existence could there be a connection with otherness?

[It is asked: "Is [this] distinct from [the pot], or non-distinct? If it is distinct, then its connection with distinctness is redundant. If it is non-distinct, even so, because of the connection with non-distinctness—which is contradictory [to distinctness]—a connection with distinctness is not possible. And since there is an absence of distinctness, the claim that 'an entity is other than the pot' is not tenable. Therefore, having taken worldly misconception as authoritative, the very nature of being a pot is established as the 'entity' (bhāva), because it is the cause for the application of the cognition and the term 'existent.
And of that..."

When form is examined in these four ways, it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, from the perspective of one who knows reality, it is established that a jar is empty of intrinsic nature, like a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*) and so forth.

To this, [the opponent] says: "The jar certainly exists, because it is the substratum (*āśraya*) of qualities (*guṇa*). For that which is non-existent is never seen to be a substratum of qualities. And the jar is indeed a substratum of qualities, as in 'one jar,' 'two jars,' and so on. Unity and the like are subsumed under the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*), while the jar is a substance (*dravya*). Furthermore, it is possible for qualities to have a substance as their substratum."
Therefore, because it is the substratum of qualities, the pot certainly exists. To this, it is replied: according to your own view.
If a single pot is not accepted, then even a pot as a unity does not arise.

If you think that a single pot does not exist because of the distinction between categories (*padārtha*), then the pot itself is not one. Just as oneness—the number one—is not the pot, so too the pot is not one because it is distinct from the number one by virtue of its substantiality (*dravyatva*). The implication is that it possesses duality [of attributes]. Furthermore, let the number one be conceptually attributed to this pot which has a single form.

Or [is it] of multiple forms? If it is of a single form, then the conceptualization of unity is entirely redundant. If, on the other hand, it is of multiple forms, then even so, it is improper because of contradiction. Therefore, in common worldly usage, the conceptualization of "one" should be understood as referring to the very nature of the jar itself, which is distinct from other non-present objects. Now, if it is argued that since qualities reside in a substance, the jar itself becomes one through its connection with unity—and not that unity becomes the jar—it is to this that we reply.
Nor is this conjunction of two equals; therefore, even by that means, one is not produced.
What is called yoga occurs only between two equal things,
not between unequal ones.

In that case, one [quality] is seen as a quality (*guṇa*) and the pot as a substance (*dravya*). Since equality does not exist between a substance and a quality, there can be no conjunction (*yoga*) between the two. Because of the absence of conjunction, the claim that "due to the conjunction with a single [quality], the pot itself becomes one" is incorrect. Furthermore, if a conjunction were observed here, then the pot would have a conjunction with the single [quality], and the single [quality] would also have a conjunction with the pot; yet since this is not the case, a conjunction between these two is simply untenable.

And because there is no conjunction, a jar does not exist as a single entity; thus, even a jar is not one. Here, the refutation is stated in the first half of the verse by accepting the [opponent's] position regarding "going" (gati); however, in the second half, the refutation is stated on the grounds of the impossibility of conjunction. Furthermore, the word "api" (even/also) should be understood as serving to aggregate the reasons for the refutation.

Moreover, this is seen to be even more illogical in the systems of others: that qualities (*guṇa*) are established as depending on substances (*dravya*), while specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) are not established as depending on [other] qualities. Yet, it is logical for qualities themselves to depend on qualities. For instance, whatever the dimension of a jar may be, its color, which depends upon that same [jar], must also be of that same extent. Consequently, it follows that color, like the substance itself, would possess magnitude (*mahattva*).
As long as a substance is form, why is that form not considered "great"?

When it is accepted by the opponent that for as much substance as there is, and for whatever configuration consisting of length and breadth a substance has, for that much is form, and for form also there is that very same configuration consisting of length and breadth, then necessarily, whether the substance be minute or large, the form therein must also possess minuteness or largeness. What then, indeed, is the reason here that the minuteness and largeness of form are not admitted in the same way as those of the substance? Now, it might be argued that form...

[Objection: "The quality of minuteness (aṇutva) and the quality of magnitude (mahattva) are indeed qualities, and it is our established tenet that there is no inherence of one quality within another quality. Therefore, even though color (rūpa) exists for as long as the substance exists, nevertheless, out of fear of contradicting our doctrine, the qualities of minuteness and magnitude do not belong to color. To this, it is replied:
If there is another opponent, the occasion for debate must be stated.
For if your opponent were indeed a member of your own school, it would be appropriate for you to state your own tenet in order to refute him; that [tenet] would then invalidate his position.

Because you lack the capacity [to respond]. However, when the opponent is another person, pointing out a contradiction with their own tenets (*siddhānta*) is ineffective against him, since his intent is directed toward refuting those very tenets. On the contrary, pointing out contradictions with reasoning (*yukti*) and worldly consensus (*loka*) is superior in that case, because it is possible to ward him off through those means. Therefore, this pointing out of a contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) is simply no defense at all; thus, that very fault remains unshakable. Consequently, there is no difference between existence (*bhāva*) and a pot (*ghaṭa*). This being so:

By the negation of the otherness of existence (*sattā*), the negation of other generalities and particulars (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth should also be understood. This is like [the negation of] number for general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*), and like [the negation of] magnitude (*mahattva*) for particularities (*viśeṣa*).

Here, it is objected: "The negation of the otherness of existence from the pot and so forth has been stated; however, since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the pot itself is not negated, the entity called 'pot' must indeed exist by way of its own form. To this, it is replied:
Where the establishment of the characterized object by means of its characteristic is not found—
such as in the case of [entities] distinct from number and so forth— in that case, the entity does not exist.

In this case, by one who asserts that the pot and its existence are characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anuvṛtti*), the exclusion-characteristic of the pot has been established by the opponent. Yet, even by means of this characteristic, the establishment of the characterized object (*lakṣya*) does not occur. For it is not possible to determine the true nature of a thing—which would then be established as the characterized object—by mere exclusion alone. To begin with, the pot is not [itself] a quality because it possesses qualities; and atoms, the large, and [the qualities such as] color and so forth are also not the pot precisely because they are qualities.

Number does not exist [independently]. Even existence (*sattā*)—due to its being a universal (*sāmānya*)—is not the pot among substances, qualities, and actions. Therefore, since this [pot] is excluded from number, magnitude, form, and so forth, it is impossible to establish that it has such an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, insofar as even by means of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) the defined (*lakṣya*)—the essential nature of the pot—is not established in the position of the opponent, in that position there exists no entity called a "pot" whose nature is established apart from number and the rest.
Consequently, it is established that the pot is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).

Alternatively, number, color, and so forth are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of a jar, because the jar is characterized by them; thus, the jar is the characterized (*lakṣya*). It is impossible to establish its own nature (*svarūpa*) as distinct from its characteristics, because its own nature is not perceived apart from number and the rest. For if that characterized nature were established, then it would necessarily be apprehended as distinct from number and the rest, such that one could say: "This is the jar's own nature, distinct from number," and "This, moreover, is its characteristic, namely number and so forth. But this is not the case; therefore [the jar has no separate nature].
Where the establishment of the characterized object through its characteristic is not found—
apart from number and so forth— in that case, the entity does not exist.
Thus, there is no pot by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

First, the refutation of the difference between the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) has been stated. However, for those whose established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the pot is identical with its form and other qualities (*rūpa*), this is said in order to refute that [position].
The jar does not possess oneness because it is not distinct from its characteristics;
since the jar is absent in each individual characteristic, multiplicity is likewise untenable.

Indeed, for those who maintain that the pot is non-different from its various characteristics such as form (rūpa) and so forth, the oneness of the pot is not tenable because it is non-different from those many characteristics of form and so on; [otherwise] there would be multiplicity due to being non-distinct from the many.

If it be thought in this regard: "If the pot does not have oneness, then alas, it must possess multiplicity," to this it is replied: Since the absence of the pot is observed in each individual characteristic such as form and so forth, therefore even multiplicity does not exist.

Here it is said: if the jar lacks unity because it is not distinct from its characteristics such as form and so forth, then the jar will possess unity through the mutual conjunction of those [characteristics]. To this, it is replied:
For indeed, there can be no conjunction of that which is intangible with that which is tangible;
therefore, a conjunction of form and the other [sensory objects] is not tenable in any way whatsoever.

In this context, "contact" (*spṛṣṭi*) means touch (*sparśa*), which is the quality of being perceivable by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). That which possesses such touch is "possessing contact" (*sparśavat*). Since the tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*) itself is perceivable by the body-faculty, it is "possessing contact. Therefore, a conjunction, union, or contact between that tangible object possessing contact and form, odor, or taste—which do not possess contact—is impossible, just as there can be no contact between a jar and space.

Since this is the case for form and the other [sensory objects], conjunction is therefore impossible in every respect. And when it is impossible, then that which was stated—that a jar is a composite based on the specific qualities of form and so forth produced by their mutual contact—is not tenable.
Now, one might argue that even without mutual contact, the mere collection of those [qualities] is the jar. This too is not the case, because:
Form is a constituent part of the jar; therefore, in that respect, it is not the jar.
Since the whole does not exist, for that reason the part is also not it.

Since the individual elements such as form (*rūpa*) constitute the parts of a jar, which is a composite form consisting of the collection of form and so forth, they do not themselves partake of the designation "jar. The jar is the whole (*avayavin*), while form and the others are its parts; thus, because form is a part, it cannot be the jar. Just as it is with form, the same should be said for odor (*gandha*) and the other qualities.

[Objection: But surely, because form (*rūpa*) consists of parts, there must exist something called a "whole" (*avayavin*). For it is not logical that parts should exist independently of a whole. [Reply: It is said in response: Since each of these factors, such as form and so forth, lacks the nature of being a jar, how could there be any whole? Indeed, apart from form and the other [sensory qualities], nothing called a "whole" can be discerned. And it is impossible to maintain the existence of that whose essential nature cannot be discerned; thus, the whole is non-existent. And since the whole does not exist, form cannot even be conceived of as a part.
Thus, the part and the whole do not exist as such. Furthermore, a pot is not a mere collection of form and so forth;
for while the nature of form (rūpatva) is indistinguishable across all forms, what indeed is the reason that the existence of "pot" applies to one form but not to others?

Regarding the phrase "of all forms" (*rūpāṇām*): because they are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), visible forms, odors, and so forth are called "forms. These forms exist even in things such as cloth, just as they do in a jar; and they do not deviate from their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) despite the difference between a jar and other objects, because they possess an identical characteristic everywhere.

In that case, just as one form exists as a pot, why is it not accepted that another form related to a cloth or other object also exists as a pot? Indeed, its existence as a pot is logical because there is no difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), just like the form and other qualities existing in a pot. However, if this is not admitted, the very cause [for designating anything as a pot] becomes impossible; consequently, either everything would attain the status of being a pot, or even the pot itself would not attain the status of being a pot.

Just as there is the consequence of non-difference for jars and the like, so too would non-difference result for visible form, odor, and the rest, because they are not other than the single jar. Now, if you think: "Even though these have no difference from the jar, nevertheless visible form has a difference from taste and the rest; therefore, the consequence of non-difference does not follow," [the author] says the following to demonstrate that this too is incorrect:
It is your view that form is distinct from taste and the other [sensory objects], but not from the pot;
yet how can that which does not exist by itself apart from them be non-different from form?

If form (*rūpa*) is established as distinct from taste (*rasa*) and the other [sensory objects] because it is apprehended by a different sense faculty, why is it not likewise established as distinct from the jar (*ghaṭa*)? Since that [jar] is not separate from form and the others—taste and so forth—it follows that, like the very nature of taste and the rest, it must be something other than form. Yet, such distinctness is not admitted; therefore, this [position] is untenable.
And when, in this way, it is impossible for form and the other [sensory objects] to be the cause of a pot, then [the following] is certain.
The pot has no cause.
Furthermore, it is not possible for that which is devoid of a cause to possess the nature of an effect by itself, being without a cause;
thus, an effect does not arise of its own accord.
And for this very reason, its being an effect without a cause is not possible.
Therefore, no pot exists as something separate from form and the other [sensory qualities].

Because a pot, which is an effect, is not perceived apart from form and the other [sensory qualities], it is established that there is no pot distinct from form and the rest.
