Now, if you think: "The pot does not indeed have form and the rest as its material cause; rather, the pot's status as an effect and the shards' status as causes are relative to their own parts," [the author] says this to show that even this is incorrect: *...ity udbhāvayann āha //* (Thus, demonstrating [this], he says: [The verse: If the pot were not perceived when its own parts are not perceived, then it would be like a forest or an army. Since it is not so, therefore the pot is not different from its own parts. [The commentary: If the pot were not perceived when its own constituent parts—the shards—are not perceived, then it would be like a forest or an army, which are merely collections of trees or soldiers. But since it is not so, therefore the pot is not different from its own parts. Furthermore, if the pot were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the pot would be perceived even when its own parts are not perceived. But such is not the case. Therefore, the pot is not different from its own parts. Nor is it the case that the pot is perceived while its own parts are not; for if it were so, then just as a forest is perceived while individual trees are not, the pot would be perceived while its own parts are not. But such is not the case. Therefore, the pot is not different from its own parts. Moreover, if the pot were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the pot would be perceived as having a different color, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the pot is not different from its own parts. Furthermore, if the pot were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the pot would be perceived as having a different shape, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the pot is not different from its own parts. And if the pot were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the pot would be perceived as having a different function, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the pot is not different from its own parts. Consequently, it is established that the pot is not different from its own parts. And because it is not different from its own parts, the pot is not different from form and the rest. Thus, it is established that there is no pot distinct from form and the rest. This concludes the refutation of the pot. Now, the refutation of the cloth follows. If the cloth were not perceived when its own parts—the threads—are not perceived, then it would be like a forest or an army. Since it is not so, therefore the cloth is not different from its own parts. If the cloth were not perceived when its own constituent parts—the threads—are not perceived, then it would be like a forest or an army, which are merely collections of trees or soldiers. But since it is not so, therefore the cloth is not different from its own parts. Furthermore, if the cloth were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the cloth would be perceived even when its own parts are not perceived. But such is not the case. Therefore, the cloth is not different from its own parts. Nor is it the case that the cloth is perceived while its own parts are not; for if it were so, then just as a forest is perceived while individual trees are not, the cloth would be perceived while its own parts are not. But such is not the case. Therefore, the cloth is not different from its own parts. Moreover, if the cloth were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the cloth would be perceived as having a different color, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the cloth is not different from its own parts. Furthermore, if the cloth were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the cloth would be perceived as having a different shape, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the cloth is not different from its own parts. And if the cloth were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the cloth would be perceived as having a different function, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the cloth is not different from its own parts. Consequently, it is established that the cloth is not different from its own parts. And because it is not different from its own parts, the cloth is not different from the threads. Thus, it is established that there is no cloth distinct from the threads. This concludes the refutation of the cloth. Now, the refutation of the atom follows. If the atom were not perceived when its own parts—parts smaller than itself—are not perceived, then it would be like a forest or an army. Since it is not so, therefore the atom is not different from its own parts. If the atom were not perceived when its own constituent parts—parts smaller than itself—are not perceived, then it would be like a forest or an army, which are merely collections of trees or soldiers. But since it is not so, therefore the atom is not different from its own parts. Furthermore, if the atom were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the atom would be perceived even when its own parts are not perceived. But such is not the case. Therefore, the atom is not different from its own parts. Nor is it the case that the atom is perceived while its own parts are not; for if it were so, then just as a forest is perceived while individual trees are not, the atom would be perceived while its own parts are not. But such is not the case. Therefore, the atom is not different from its own parts. Moreover, if the atom were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the atom would be perceived as having a different color, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the atom is not different from its own parts. Furthermore, if the atom were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the atom would be perceived as having a different shape, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the atom is not different from its own parts. And if the atom were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the atom would be perceived as having a different function, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the atom is not different from its own parts. Consequently, it is established that the atom is not different from its own parts. And because it is not different from its own parts, the atom is not different from its own constituent parts. Thus, it is established that there is no atom distinct from its own constituent parts. This concludes the refutation of the atom. Now, the refutation of the whole follows. If the whole were not perceived when its own parts are not perceived, then it would be like a forest or an army. Since it is not so, therefore the whole is not different from its own parts. If the whole were not perceived when its own constituent parts are not perceived, then it would be like a forest or an army, which are merely collections of trees or soldiers. But since it is not so, therefore the whole is not different from its own parts. Furthermore, if the whole were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the whole would be perceived even when its own parts are not perceived. But such is not the case. Therefore, the whole is not different from its own parts. Nor is it the case that the whole is perceived while its own parts are not; for if it were so, then just as a forest is perceived while individual trees are not, the whole would be perceived while its own parts are not. But such is not the case. Therefore, the whole is not different from its own parts. Moreover, if the whole were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the whole would be perceived as having a different color, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the whole is not different from its own parts. Furthermore, if the whole were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the whole would be perceived as having a different shape, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the whole is not different from its own parts. And if the whole were different from its own parts, then just as a forest is different from the trees, the whole would be perceived as having a different function, etc., from its own parts. But such is not the case. Therefore, the whole is not different from its own parts. Consequently, it is established that the whole is not different from its own parts. And because it is not different from its own parts, the whole is not different from its own constituent parts. Thus, it is established that there is no whole distinct from its own constituent parts. This concludes the refutation of the whole. Now, the refutation of the universal follows. If the universal were not perceived when its own particulars are not perceived, then it would be like a forest
The pot is established through its cause, and the cause is established through another;
how can that which has no establishment of itself produce another?

If the pot is established in dependence upon its causes, the shards, then in turn, in dependence upon what are those shards established? For they are certainly not established by way of their own intrinsic nature.

[Otherwise,] there would be the undesirable consequence of [the pot] being causeless. If, on the other hand, another cause is postulated for those [shards], then the essential nature of the shards themselves is not established, because they too depend upon other causes, such as gravel. Since those shards whose own nature is not established cannot establish anything else by way of their own nature, for this reason also the pot is non-existent. Furthermore, this very same formal argument that negates the pot may be applied to the non-establishment of all effects.
To this, he says: "The designation 'pot' applies to the collection of form and so forth."

"Even if there is a multiplicity of color-forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, it does not follow that there is a multiplicity of pots. This too is incorrect, because the collection itself is non-existent. For it is thus:
Even in the case of inherence, the nature of smell cannot belong to form;
therefore, the unity of a collection is not tenable, just as it is not for a jar.

Even when combined, form and the other [sensory objects] do not abandon their respective individual characteristics during the state of aggregation. Consequently, because form does not relinquish its own nature during the state of aggregation, the quality of "odor-ness" cannot possibly exist [in that same form]. Likewise, the unity of a collection based on multiple substrata is not conceivable.

For that collection is not distinct from form and the others, and those forms and so forth are mutually differentiated. Since the collection is not distinct from form and the others, how could it be one? He provides an illustration: "just as in the case of a jar. Just as...
It has been stated that a jar does not possess oneness because it is not distinct from its characteristics; likewise here too,
the collection does not possess oneness because it is not distinct from its characteristics.
Thus, in this way, the unity of a collection is not tenable, just as it is not tenable for a jar;
and consequently, since a collection is impossible, the conceptualization of a "jar" even within a collection of form and so forth is not logical, according to the analysis already described.
Just as a jar does not exist apart from its form and other qualities,
so too form does not exist apart from air and the other elements.

Just as a jar is not established apart from form and the other [sensory objects], so too form and the others—which are the basis for the designation "jar"—are not tenable apart from the four great elements, such as wind and the rest; for that would entail the consequence of their being causeless.

And just as form, smell, and so forth cannot exist apart from wind and the other [elements], so too, because the great elements cannot be established apart from one another, he says this while demonstrating the non-establishment of form and the others:
Fire itself becomes hot; how could that which is not hot be burned?
Therefore, there is no such thing as fuel, and without it, fire does not exist.

In this context, fire is the burner and the three elements are the fuel to be burned. Thus, this triad of elements known as "fuel" is burned by fire alone and nothing else; and it is the fuel alone that is burned, and nothing else. In that regard, if fire burns the fuel through its heat, then it is fire itself that possesses that heat, not the fuel. Since burning is impossible for that which is not hot, even that which is not hot cannot be fuel. Therefore, since the object to be burned is in every respect non-existent, there is no such thing as "fuel" consisting of the triad of elements.

And when, in this way, fuel cannot exist as something other than fire, then in the absence of fuel, fire—being without a cause—cannot exist either; thus, "without that [fuel], fire is not found. Here [the opponent] says: Fuel is indeed of a non-hot nature because its form consists of solidity and so forth. That [fuel] becomes hot due to being overwhelmed by fire, which has heat as its intrinsic nature. And being hot, it burns. Even if it is conceptualized in this manner, the entity called "fuel" [remains problematic].
If that which is overcome were also hot, why would it not be produced as fire?

If it is imagined that the object called fuel, though its intrinsic nature is not hot, becomes hot when overcome by fire, then let that fire also be non-hot in its essential form; and consequently, it would simply be the absence of fuel.
Furthermore, it is not tenable that existence also resides in fire which is not hot.

Now, even if it is maintained that this object, though overcome [by fire], is indeed non-hot, then it would follow that the other constituent of fire—the triad of elements called "fuel"—must also exist within fire with a non-hot nature, because it is opposed to heat. Consequently, fire would be nothing more than the mere absence of the triad of elements. Yet, these great elements do not exist apart from one another; if they did, it would contradict established doctrine. Furthermore, since the other entity called fuel would be absent in fire, fire itself would be causeless; therefore, this position is untenable.
Now, if you think that because the three elements are absent in the atom of the substance fire, fire exists even without fuel, it is said in reply:
If there is no fuel for the atom, then fire exists without fuel.

Consequently, that very same fault of causelessness [applies]. Precisely because of this consequence of the fault of causelessness, the acceptance of substantial atoms by those of our own school is untenable, just as it is for the Vaiśeṣikas. Furthermore, since the Vaiśeṣika doctrine of atoms has already been refuted in the ninth chapter, it is not refuted again here.
It is just as if one were to postulate the existence of fuel-atoms out of fear of the consequence that fire would be causeless.
An atom does not exist as a single entity, for it too would have fuel [as its constituent parts].
If it is conceived that there is fuel within the atom, then it must not be accepted that the fire-element atom exists as a single-natured entity.
Furthermore, it is not only the atom that lacks a unitary nature; for indeed, due to the rule that the eight substances arise simultaneously, other categories of entities likewise lack such unity.
Whichever entity is examined, that very thing possesses no singularity.

Just as there is no single self-nature among the primary elements (*bhūta*) because each exists only in relation to the others, so too a derivative element (*bhautika*) does not exist in isolation, for that would entail the consequence of it being causeless. Likewise, mental factors (*caitta*) do not occur without the mind (*citta*), nor does the mind occur without mental factors. Similarly, the characterized object (*lakṣya*), such as form (*rūpa*), does not exist without its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), such as birth (*jāti*) and the rest; nor can a characteristic exist without the characterized object, as it would then be without a basis.

And since, in this way, there is no establishment of any single entity whatsoever, then—in the absence of a collection of single units—the establishment of multiple entities is also utterly discarded; thus he says:
Because that by which even one does not exist, therefore even many do not exist.
When one [of the two] is unestablished, there is no establishment even for the collection [of both].

Now, it might be argued that this refutation applies only to one's own school (svayūthya), because they accept the rule of simultaneous arising; however, for an opponent, this is not a refutation, since they accept the existence of eternal atoms of earth and so forth as being devoid of the presence of any other entity. To demonstrate the incorrectness even in that case, he says:
If it is thought that the other three entities do not exist there, but one does exist;
This too is incorrect.
What is the reason?
Since there is a state of threefoldness everywhere, therefore a state of oneness does not exist.

For even for the opponent, there is no such thing as a single entity whatsoever; because even in that case, within an atom of earth, there exists this triad: substantiality (*dravyatva*), unity (*ekatva*), and existence (*sattva*). Likewise, in a quality (*guṇa*), there is the triad of quality-ness (*guṇatva*), existence, and unity. Since this triad exists, there is no such thing as a single entity. Thus, for the Sāṃkhya, who holds that everything consists of the three *guṇas*, there is no single entity at all; therefore, no objection stated [against the Buddhist position] can bypass this [Sāṃkhya view].
Furthermore, teaching that this method of refutation should be employed by the learned to overturn the positions of all disputants, the Master says:
"Real, unreal, both real and unreal, and neither real nor unreal"— this sequence should always be applied by the wise regarding oneness and the other categories.
Oneness, otherness, both, and neither—these are "oneness and so forth. When these positions, such as oneness and the rest, have been established by the proponent, he...

The sequence of refutations, characterized by the [arguments] beginning with "the ten," should be applied in due order by the wise one. In this regard, the position of the proponent of the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavādin*) is that cause and effect are identical. For according to him, that effect, while already established in the form of the cause, merely undergoes transformation into the form of the effect; for it is impossible to produce what is non-existent. If indeed the non-existent were to arise, then everything would be possible from everything. Yet, it is not observed that everything arises from everything.

Because we observe that curd and so forth arise specifically from milk and so forth, this proponent—who accepts the identity of cause and effect—holds the position of identity according to which an already existent effect is produced. Regarding that position of identity, a refutation must always be stated based on the consideration of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). And this has been said:
"The decoration of pillars and such would be useless for the purpose of a house."
By the statement,
"For whom the effect is held to exist [even before production]," it is shown that it is not logical to say that something exists prior to its coming into being.
If birth were to exist for one who already exists, then existence would also exist for one who has already been born.
If dharma exists even when unperformed, then the rule [of action] is rendered futile; yet if even the slightest thing must be performed, then the existence of a pre-existent effect is impossible.
Thus it has been said.
CHAPTER XV: Refutation of the Meaning of the Conditioned (saṃskṛta).
For one who is being born, there is no origination, because there would have to be an interval even for that.

For that proponent for whom there is no possibility of the two—past and future—without an interval (*antara*) or a middle (*madhya*), for him there is no "presently arising" (*jāyamāna*). How so? Because there would have to be an interval for that as well. Just as the "presently arising" exists within the interval between the past and the future, so too this "presently arising"—which possesses the nature of being both arisen and unarisen—must have a middle, in dependence upon which the distinction between the arisen and the unarisen could be established. And it is impossible to establish a third thing called "presently arising" in the interval between the arisen and the unarisen.

[Objection: In every case, because the conceptualization of a "being-born" (*jāyamāna*) between what is already born and what is not yet born would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), [the opponent] says: "The 'being-born' is certainly not half-born, for then the aforementioned fault would follow. What then? That entity which, through its cessation, becomes a 'born' thing (*padārtha*), is that entity existing in a state prior to birth which is called 'being-born'. Demonstrating this very point, he says:

Since that which is already born arises through the cessation of that which is being born, the existence of something other than that [already born] is likewise seen in the case of what is being born.
Since an entity becomes "already born" through the cessation of that which is "being born," it follows that even apart from the half-born state, the entity that is "being born" must indeed exist.
To this, it is replied:
When something has already arisen, there is no possibility of its being in the process of arising.

For as long as this entity is said to be "arisen," at that time it is not "in the process of arising. And because that which is in the process of arising does not exist, the state of being "arisen" itself does not exist. Therefore, one might infer the "process of arising" by means of the "arisen. Now, if even that which is "arisen" were to be "in the process of arising," then for that [entity], the impossibility of its production would follow.
Demonstrating that it is because of reality, he says:
Why is that which has already been born born again when it is in the process of being born?

When that which is already born is called "being born," then one might wonder from what that "being born" object arises. The intention [of the author] is that since it is already established, the conceptualization of its arising is not tenable; therefore, it is not logical to say that "the being born is born. To this, he says: Even though it is unborn, because it is oriented toward birth, it is called "being born" and is thus "born. Consequently, that which is "being born" is indeed "born," and its arising is not purposeless. Even so, if...
The unborn is indeed called "born," and that which is being born is said to be "made."

If an entity that is as yet unborn is conceptualized by another as "born" because it is facing birth, then since there is no difference between the born and the unborn, why is the pot not then conceptualized as non-existence?

For it is only an entity in the state of having been born that is designated as "a jar. And since there is identity between the born and the unborn, it would follow that even a born jar is a non-entity due to its prior non-existence; yet this is not possible, so this [position] is incorrect. Furthermore, it might be argued: "There is no absence of distinction between the being-born and the unborn. For an entity undergoing the action of arising is called 'being-born,' and that..."
Although not yet fully accomplished, that which is being born is excluded from the unborn.
Even though an object that has not yet reached completion is established as being external while it is in the process of arising,
nevertheless, it arises as something unborn, since it is excluded from what has already been born.

Just as that which is being born is excluded from what has already been born because it is outside the scope of activity (*kriyāveśa*) due to its unestablished nature, so too it is excluded even from that which is currently being born; consequently, it follows that only the unborn is born, and thus there is no such thing as "that which is being born.

Furthermore, it is not only because of being external to what has already been born that only the unborn is born; for this reason as well, only the unborn is born: because [the activity] belongs to another.
Even when being born, it did not exist previously, and indeed it does not exist afterwards;
therefore, by that [process], the unborn is born.

The word *āsīt* denotes something that occurred long ago; it means "it was not," or "it did not exist. That which is currently designated as being in the process of arising (*jāyamāna*) did not exist [previously]. Here, the word *prāk* (before) functions as a term of limit. Prior to the present state, in the past time, that object which is now arising was non-existent; yet, it is said that it subsequently comes to be born. Therefore, even though it is unborn, it is called "arising" at the very moment it enters into the activity of birth. Consequently, by virtue of its being unborn, it possesses the quality of having been non-existent (*abhūtatva*).
And since an originating action cannot proceed without a basis for that which is non-existent and has not yet attained its own nature, he says:
That which is non-existent is not born.
Thus it is said.
Moreover:
That which has arisen and exists is called "perfected," while that which does not exist is called "unconditioned."

By the term "exists" (*asti*), the perfected (*niṣpanna*) is expressed; for it is only when an entity is perfected that the thought "it exists" arises. "Exists" has the meaning of "becomes. By the term "does not exist" (*nāsti*), the uncreated and unperfected is expressed. Apart from these two states, [there is nothing else].
When he was being born, what indeed was that state called?

Thus, when an entity in the state of being born—such that one cannot designate it as "this object exists"—cannot be defined, it is logical to conclude that it is indeed non-existent because its own nature is not being determined. Therefore, by the analysis described above, that which is in the process of arising is impossible.
When the effect does not exist apart from its cause,
then neither its arising nor its cessation is possible.

When an effect that is distinct from its cause is analyzed and found to be impossible, then activity—namely the arising of the effect and the cessation of the cause—is no longer possible, as it would be without a basis. Thus, when phenomena are examined in this way, they are not established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, the very likeness of an illusion remains for all phenomena. This illusion, which speaks to the foolish, deludes those who are ignorant.

Having understood that which causes wonder even to those who are not deluded, and having shaken off this thirst for things arising from the dogmatic attachment to what is unreal, he brought face-to-face the triad of great compassion, the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and non-dual gnosis—which serve as the seeds for the arising of supreme gnosis—for the sake of benefiting the entire world. Having correctly ascertained the nature of saṃsāra, he beheld the world—situated within the house of the three realms, which is being consumed by the rows of flames of the fire of afflictions and suffering, and is without protection—as it undergoes various transformations moment by moment due to the convergence of all the misfortunes of the world condensed into one.

Furthermore, even though cyclic existence brings about the simultaneous onset of all the sufferings of the entire world gathered together, one who is undaunted by these afflictions of body and mind—even throughout the duration of *saṃsāra*—should maintain each moment of heroic vigor. Having understood that for the wise, birth in existence is the cause for the arising of the treasure-store of the jewel of the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā-jñāna*), and desiring to share this with the entire world through the arising of such knowledge, it is indeed fitting to take up existence once again.
In the Bodhisattvayogācāra-catuḥśataka, the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Refutation of the Meaning of the Conditioned."

Having completed the work of the treatise through the fifteen preceding chapters, having established the purpose for the commencement of the treatise, and demonstrating the resolution of other remaining points, he begins the sixteenth chapter.
Due to some cause, that which is empty appears as if it were non-empty;
its negation is established through all the relevant contexts.

No one is able, without first determining emptiness as it truly is, to cast off attachment to cyclic existence and generate a longing for nirvāṇa. Furthermore, because the meaning of emptiness causes extreme terror among worldly beings, it must be introduced by a wise person skilled in communicating unpleasant news—just as a messenger might produce a sense of composure in a king by announcing the death of his beloved wife through some skillful means. For the world, distorted by the delusions of "I-making," "mine-making," and craving, perceives the mere flow of conditioned formations as permanent, due to its failure to see their momentary disintegration.

Because he fails to determine the meaning of "mine," he apprehends permanence—which acts as an obstacle to the vision of emptiness—and thus maintains that the world is indeed non-empty. Therefore, the commencement of this first chapter is for the purpose of refuting his [view of] non-emptiness; this is how the passage beginning with these words should be construed. Furthermore, it has been stated more than once that the meaning of "emptiness" here is the state of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Thus, for those who perceive that a thing is indeed non-empty despite being devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) due to some cause, the negation of that false apprehension is established by all fifteen chapters.

If it is argued that the commencement of these chapters is for this very purpose, does it not follow that the non-emptiness of entities is thereby established? For in this way, there is first of all you, the speaker of these chapters; and there is the subject matter of the chapters, which is non-emptiness; and there is the cause that turns back the cause [of the opponent's] position.

Demonstrating that this statement—which consists of a collection of sounds with distinct meanings and limits, and which comprises fifteen chapters—is indeed existent because of the presence of the speaker, the subject matter, and the speech itself, [the author] says the following to show that your laborious effort in beginning all these chapters is entirely in vain: [and thus the non-emptiness of entities is established].
When there is a speaker and that which is to be spoken, it is not empty.
